Operators displaying zero-dimensional spectral properties inherently arise within the framework of ergodic Schr\"odinger operators. We establish a refined definition of a complete family of Hausdorff measure functions specifically designed to meticulously analyze and differentiate these singular measures with adjustable precision. In the analysis, we establish that the dimensionality for spectral measures associated with positive Lyapunov exponents in single-sided operators never exceeds logarithmic levels, regardless of the specific boundary phase involved. We further complement this theoretical bound by providing a constructive counter-example—an explicit operator whose spectral measure achieves this maximal dimension. Finally, we generalize and upgrade several foundational theorems concerning rank one perturbations and quantum evolution by extending them into the domain of generalized Hausdorff dimensions.

This study explores fluctuations and dissipative behavior within a deformable anti-de Sitter space at high temperature and finite density, where the spacetime geometry corresponds to a charged black hole arising from Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton action. Incorporating horizon function backreaction due to the exponential space deformation, we compute the admittance while analyzing the impacts of temperature and chemical potential. Furthermore, by deriving two-point correlation functions and mean square displacements for both bosons and fermions, we extract short- and long-time asymptotic limits; notably, the long-time regime exhibits a logarithmic sub-diffusion proportional to $\log t$. Finally, utilizing results from both the admittance and correlation analyses, we verify the fluctuation-dissipation theorem applicable to these bosonic and fermionic frameworks.

This paper establishes the theory of weak sharp minima (WSM) within the context of convex interval-valued functions (IVFs). To characterize these minima, the work offers both primal and dual descriptions. Specifically, the primal characterization utilizes $gH$-directional derivatives, while the derivation of conditions relies upon a dual approach. This dual strategy involves introducing $gH$-subdifferentiability and the concept of support functions for subsets of $I(\mathbb{R})^n$ tailored to convex IVFs, alongside an established $gH$-subdifferential calculus for such functions. Ultimately, by leveraging this refined calculus, the paper delivers the desired dual characterizations for the sets of WSM for convex IVFs.

Multi-modality yields valuable complementary information for clinical prediction, yet missing data within clinical cohorts frequently restricts the number of participants suitable for multi-modal analysis. Achieving missing data imputation in a multi-modality setting remains difficult using current methods under two primary circumstances: when data is missing across heterogeneous modalities (e.g., image versus textual or tabular), or when a single modality suffers substantial missingness. In this study, we propose a novel imputation strategy grounded in modeling the joint distribution of multi-modality inputs and previously inspired partially by Partial Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks (PBiGAN). We introduce a Conditional PBiGAN (C-PBIGNet) model that exploits conditional signals from one pathway to reconstruct missing data within the complementary modality. Specifically, the C-PBIGNet incorporates a shared latent representation for accessible multi-modality features into its imputation pipeline and applies discriminative constraints via classification losses within these reconstructed regions. To the best of our awareness, this remains the first Generative Adversarial Network specifically tailored to address multi-modality gaps by explicitly modeling the distribution of image-based and non-image data. Validation using both the National Lung Screening Trial dataset and an external clinical cohort confirms that the C-PBIGNet dramatically improves lung cancer risk prediction relative to standard imputation baselines; the model demonstrated higher areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve compared to standard PBiGANG, with increases totaling +3% and +5% compared controls (p<0.1).

Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) remains a reliable platform for creating entangled states, yet it conventionally necessitates a coherent laser pump to interact with a nonlinear crystal. In this study, we circumvent this requirement to produce polarization-entangled photon pairs by utilizing a standard light-emitting diode (LED) as the pump source. At first glance, this approach seems counterintuitive given the LED's very low spatial coherence; however, this incoherence is mapped onto the resulting biphoton wavefunction. Nevertheless, type-II phase-matching intrinsically filters the LED emission to specific wavelengths satisfying the down-conversion condition. This mechanism enables the generation of localized polarization Bell states even without global coherence across the full transverse area. In this experiment, we assess the fidelity of the LED-driven entanglement according to standard criteria by measuring Bell inequality violation. The achieved Bell state parameter was $S=2.33\pm 0.097$, which decisively exceeds the classical limit of $S=2$, thereby confirming quantum entanglement. These findings demonstrate that similar sources of "natural light"—including sunlight and bioluminescent sources—can also be harnessed to prepare polarization entanglement, potentially paving the way for electric-free quantum communication in deep-space environments.

Theories regarding the spontaneous wavefunction collapse aim to explain why the laws of quantum mechanics might fail at macroscopic scales. Yet, conclusive verification has previously been unachievable due to the difficulty in detecting predicted collapse signals above noise. In this work, we propose to solve this by using a superconducting qubit to accurately measure the temperature increases induced by collapse in a mechanical resonator. We demonstrate that achieving strong entanglement between a qubit and resonator allows for both rapid measurements and robust ground-state preparation, effectively suppressing dominant noise sources like quasiparticle heating. Furthermore, our predictions show that bulk acoustic wave resonances can enhance the observable collapse-heating effects through exceptionally low energy loss. Collectively, these capabilities could provide a definitive test of wavefunction collapse models.

Inferring galaxy attenuation curves frequently relies on spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, in which dust attenuation is estimated concurrently with other physical galactic parameters. This paper evaluates how SED modeling can derive such dust curves from broadband photometry and introduces a novel, flexible approach to significantly enhance derivation accuracy. By fitting mock SEDs produced by the Simba cosmological simulation using the Prospector code within this framework, we examine both the widely used uniform screen assumption and our new proposal: a non-uniform screen model defined by the proportion of unobscured stellar emission. This non-uniform approach permits a fraction of starlight to pass unattenuated, offering a more adaptable attenuation profile by severing the strict coupling between the ultraviolet (UV) and optical curve shapes. Adopting this non-uniform screen substantially sharpens constraints on the attenuation curve; the UV median offset in attenuation improves, dropping from -0.30 dex under the uniform screen assumption to only -0.17 dex with the non-uniform variant. This enhanced modeling precision also refines star formation rate (SFR) estimations, with the mean SFR offset reducing by 0.12 dex on average using our new model. Finally, we assess the effectiveness of this methodology, addressing limitations in modeling stellar-dust geometries and the constraints imposed by current SED observational data.

Research area ontologies have demonstrated significant utility in interpreting and analyzing scholarly datasets. This chapter introduces the Computer Science Ontology (CSO), representing the most extensive ontology of computer scientific domains available. It examines multiple practical applications derived from the CSO that enable high-level functions, including metadata retrieval, subject classification, and the curation or suggestion of academic books.

Conventional constant-height differential conductance spectroscopy conducted in the high bias regime, where the voltage surpasses the sample's work function, fails to accurately reflect the local density of states (LDOS) because the tunneling barrier conditions vary. Although high applied voltages often make constant-height measurements experimentally unfeasible, resulting in a practical preference for constant-current spectroscopy, this approach introduces its own inaccuracy as variations in tunnel current necessitate changing tip positions, further deviating from the true LDOS. This article introduces a novel normalization protocol designed to extract the LDOS from high bias scattering tunneling spectroscopy performed under both constant-height and constant-current conditions. The framework is expanded to consider the in-plane momentum contributions of the probed electronic states. The effectiveness of this method is verified through application to laterally confined field-emission resonances, presenting well-defined in-plane momentum peak-like structures in the resulting conductance spectra.

Recent studies have achieved significant success in neural style transfer, but most methods limit stylization to the pixel domain, an approach deemed imperfect as real paintings are composed of brushstrokes rather than pixels. This work argues for moving to brushstroke-level stylization and proposes a method that optimizes parametric strokes while introducing a differentiable rendering module. This approach not only achieves significantly superior visual quality but also affords greater control over the stylization flow through user interaction. Both quantitative and qualitative results confirm that utilizing a parametric representation is an efficacious strategy.

Affective polarization describes the growing trend in many democracies where citizens harbor intense negativity toward out-party members and their policies. This phenomenon arises largely from economic struggle, social disparity, and racial or group-based conflicts, especially when these grievances map closely onto existing party alignments. This paper employs cultural evolution modeling to demonstrate how economic forces fuel both identity sorting along partisan lines and the affective division itself, ultimately amplifying pre-existing group inequalities on a feedback loop. However, our analysis offers an optimistic counterbalance: we find that generous levels of wealth redistribution, achieved via public goods provision, can disrupt this cycle and curb rising resentment. Finally, the study's core hypotheses validate against survey data spanning the past half-century of racial sorting and affective polarization in the United States.

We present the Oracle-MNIST dataset, a benchmark for pattern classification comprising 28$\times $28 grayscale representations of 30,222 ancient characters across 10 categories. The training phase involves 27,222 images, while the test set allocates 300 samples per class, specifically addressing the difficulties of image noise, distortion, and aging spanning three millennia due to burial processes. These challenges, combined with the dramatically varying handwriting styles found among ancient Chinese calligraphy, make the data realistically demanding for machine learning. Compatible directly with all standard classifiers through the same data structure as the original MNIST, Oracle-MNUST serves as a more complex alternative for this specific task and is available at https://github.com/wm-bupt/oracle-mnist.

We introduce Typography-MNIST (TMNIST), a comprehensive dataset containing over 555,238,239 grayscale MNIST-inspired images that depict more than 1,812 distinct glyphs across various designs drawn from 1,386,370 Google Fonts. This extensive glyph collection includes common characters spanning over 151 contemporary and ancient writing systems; importantly, different stylistic variations of fonts are represented by subsets of these unique glyphs. Created within the CognitiveType initiative, this dataset facilitates the construction of real-time eye-tracking tools designed to map typography to cognition, alongside computational frameworks to facilitate user-friendly typeface creation with optimized readability properties. Both the dataset and the specialized script library used to generate styled glyphs into MNIST-images are open-source and accessible at the GitHub repository for CognitiveType.

Given that prompt diagnosis and intervention are the most critical components of Cerebral Palsy (CP) therapy, developing a highly effective and transparent automatic prediction system is vital. We identify notable discrepancies in the human movement frequencies of CP infants compared to healthy individuals—a feature that notably boosts prediction accuracy, yet this frequency data remains underutilized in prevailing deep learning methodologies designed to predict CP. This study introduces a Frequency Attention-Informed Graph Convolutional Network (FA-GCN) and empirically evaluates its use across two consumer-level RGB video datasets: MINI-RGBD and RVI-38. Empirical tests indicate our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on both datasets. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the benefits of leveraging frequency data for non-invasive CP prediction, offering a practical solution to assist with diagnosis in areas where medical expertise and resources are scarce.

With a global pivot toward data-centric industries, there is surging demand for automated algorithms that can transform digitally scanned documents into machine-readable content. This technology not only facilitates data digitization for advanced analytics but also substantially automates workflows previously reliant on manual review. While optical character recognition effectively converts text images into readable characters, extracting comprehensive table structures remains less refined. Table processing involves two core challenges: detection and structure recognition. Although prior research has addressed these individually, few offers a unifying end-to-end approach capable of handling practical issues like noise and image rotation. Currently, trends favor deep learning combined with transfer learning for structure recognition to address data scarcity. This study presents **Multi-Type-TD-TSR**, an end-to-end pipeline for full table recognition that employs state-of-the-art deep models for detection and distinguishes among three table categories based on bordering styles. Structure recognition utilizes deterministic, non-data-driven base algorithms tailored either for bordered or unbordered tables. Evaluated on the ICDAR 2019 Table Structure Recognition dataset, Multi-Type-TD-TSR establishes a new state of the art in performance.

Evaluation across Dbpedia and FinegraNing Entities from Relations (FIGER), benchmarked on both coarse and fine-class categories, highlights the superiority of this approach over baseline methods. We employ a variational perturbation framework based on Lagrangians, using a specific functional form and subsequent validation via the split-step Fourier method. A key objective was to define system conditions ensuring dynamic stability across both negative and positive index regimes of these materials. Similar to standard media, 3D light pulses are generally unstable in Kerr-only nonlinear metamaterials. Uniquely, however, in the negative index regime, stable propagation is achievable within the normal dispersion range when balanced defocusing cubic and focusing quintic nonlinearities coexist. Similarly, in the positive index regime, achieving stable dynamics requires focusing cubic and defocusing quintic nonlinearities within the anomalously dispersive domain. Furthermore, we assessed the soliton character by simulating collisions between two bullets. Our numerical findings indicate that, much like their counterparts with cubo-quartic nonlinear properties, 3D spatio-temporal soliton pulses remain invariant except for possible phase shifts after colliding in environments featuring both cubic and quintic effects in opposing signs. But if the balance between dispersion and nonlinearity falters, interactions lead to the creation of distorted soliton molecules laden with high energy levels; ultimately, oscillations intensify, degrading the bullets into unstable filament structures. Notably, we replicated identical collision dynamics in the metamaterials, whatever their specific refractive indexing regime, positive or negative.

Ultrastrong coupling, an electromagnetic regime where optical and material excitations interact intensely, facilitates diverse physical phenomena. Historically, this phenomenon has relied on quantum emitters like organic dyes, quantum wells, artificial atoms in superconductors, or transitions in two-dimensional electron gases. Typically, accessing this regime necessitates stringent conditions such as high vacuum, powerful magnetic fields, and ultra-low temperatures. However, a recent document suggests that a high level of light-matter coupling is achievable under ambient conditions using plasmonic meta-atoms—artificial metallic nanostructures designed to supplant traditional quantum emitters. Despite advancements, definitive limits on coupling strength within these systems remained unidentified. Employing a theoretical Hamiltonian framework, this study analyzes the formation of polaritonic states and establishes theoretical caps on the individual and collective plasmon-photon interaction strengths within arrays of densely packed plasmonic meta-atoms. Research initially performed on spherical forms identified universal upper bounds for the normalized coupling ratio $g/\omega_0$, representing ensembles versus free-space photons. Subsequent investigations into spheroidal configurations demonstrated that a highly elongated metal nanostructure maximizes collective interaction in a meta-atom array. These findings hold significant promise for polaritonics, quantum technology applications, and the synthesis materials.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are now state-of-the-art for various machine learning tasks, including the analysis of proteins, social networks, and chemical molecules. Because some of the corresponding datasets hold sensitive information, applying machine learning via differential privacy (DP) offers a promising path to extracting insights while providing formal privacy protections. The private training of GNNs, however, remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the difficulties arising from graphs' inherent structural connectivity. This study presents an adaptation of DP methods for graph-level classification, a central task within the realm of graph machine learning, specifically devised for deep learning on multi-graph data using differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). The approach evaluates results on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets, analyzing how GNN architectures and hyperparameters influence performance in private settings. Ultimately, explainability techniques are employed to verify the similarity of model representations learned with and without privacy protections, thereby setting robust baseline metrics for future research in this domain.

Robotic guide dogs offer distinct benefits regarding production costs and scalability compared to biological canines, yet earlier research on these automation systems frequently overlooked the handler-dog team dynamics essential for navigation. To construct a truly helpful robotic guiding system, we conducted field work comprising interviews with handlers and their trainers alongside directed walking experiments while wearing a blindfold, leveraging insights gained primarily from these experiential and interview methods. We developed a cooperative navigation protocol grounded in this real-world data that prioritizes user-requested functionality such as precise speed modulation and direction setting. Our solution centers on a contextually intelligent local planning module, which leverages environmental semantic data alongside the handler's positional and orientation cues to calculate safe routes while keeping the handler free from obstacles; we validated the efficacy and behavior of our integrated system through indoor bench trials featuring guided walking, successfully replicating natural avoidance maneuvers at a pace typical for guide work of 0.7 m/s.

By incorporating all relevant relativistic effects, our work has formulated an entirely nonlinear, gauge-invariant framework to model cosmological observables. This system derives the second-order corrections regarding light propagation, distinct from previous gauge-specific choices, ensuring no arbitrary gauge-conditioning during description. This paper presents the primary full validation of such expressions by demonstrating, via an independent verification of gauge transformation properties sourced through both metric perturb approaches and nonlinear relations expectations, that these theoretical behaviors are mathematically equivalent and satisfy consistency requirements. We confirm invariance under diffeomorphic variations in observed-space values for various observables such as the clustering nature of galaxies and measured brightness distances. By engaging a series with prior literature, it further highlights these findings through subtle distinctions in pertaining descriptions. This second-grade, gauge-invariant structure marks a significant progression within modern cosmological refinement fields and will be critical to analyzing early universe aspects of evolution beyond standard Power spectrum predictions.

Multilevel linear models enable the flexible analysis of complex data characterized by hierarchical stratifications, though selecting the optimal model from a vast pool of candidates remains difficult. While the standard Bayesian approach compares models via model evidence (or Bayes factors), direct calculations using these metrics—feasible mainly for simple linear models with restrictive priors—are often impossible due to complexity. Consequently, techniques like sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo are commonly employed, yet evaluating their reliability can be uncertain. This paper proposes a method to estimate the log-evidence through the marginalisation of intermediate parameters that relate to non-variance aspects, which simplifies sampling dimensions for improved estimation consistency. We aim to clarify how this framework integrates functionally in practical applications involving hierarchical data. The approach is validated using both simulated multilevel examples and a widely used dataset of residential radon radiation levels from Minnesota.

Next-generation detectors aimed at weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) will confront a formidable hurdle: their ability to sense coherent scattering from solar neutrinos, necessitating robust methods to distinguish signal from background. Directional detectors are proposed to overcome both WIMP detection sensitivity limits and the irreducible neutrino background, with wide-bandgap semiconductors offering a route for dense targeting. These devices operate by combining a real-time collection of phonon, photon, or electric charge upon energy deposition with the creation of stable, kilometer-scale damage tracks within the host lattice that preserve directional data. These latent patterns are later retrieved using atomic physics methods spanning quantum defect sensing to X-ray microscopy. Currently, they detail this detection concept and the current experimental capabilities for readable nuclear tracks. The focus falls on diamonds, given its central position in quantum innovation and semiconductor advancement and by virtue of experimental developments within it, they posit that future decades might lead new techniques toward refined dark matter and astrophysical measurements and motivate interdisciplinary innovation.

This paper tackles image instance semantic segmentation through weak supervision solely utilizing instance-wise labels to derive boundary masks. A frequent method involves propagating class activation map (CAM) scores via random walks. However, as a feed-forward operation without explicit constraints or a random component, it can produce low-quality pseudo labels with limited regularization for the training set without full supervision. To mitigate this, we introduce an image-specific feature propagation framework that leverages graph convolutional nets (GCNs). Formulated as a semi-supervised problem, we generate coarse segmentation masks for every image as input. Each image utilizes a separate two-layer GCN for propagation that trains the graph Laplacian mechanism and entropy loss function. Furthermore, experimental evidence from the VOC-12 dataset further verifies the efficacy of our scheme in comparison with current state-of-the-art approaches. Fonts appear frequently in digital documents, available in numerous visual styles. These are typically defined as native vectors converted into a non-standard format or rasterized into pixelated images of fixed resolution. The non-standard vector approach limits adoption of state-of-the-art neural network architectures for representation, whereas standard encoding of the resulting image data causes fidelity losses because edges, sharp angles, other geometric subtleties are effectively absent, which makes them challenging for neural networks to accurately represent. Since complex font representations can be decomposed into a set of implicit occupancy distributions, we present Multi-Implicit to accurately represent fonts using a permutation-invariant group of implicit functions that retain critical information. Local features (such as sharp angles) can be effectively preserved in a multi-parameter form without significant feature reduction or significant signal fluctuation. To obtain effective local training signals when global multi-parameter signals are present, we use an alternative approach that utilizes a partially localized signal during the neural network's training to reveal an output. For local features (such as sharp edges), we use global-local inference with neural network representations of font families. Finally, we present various applications, including style-consistent rendering of font families where individual glyphs are used for complete reconstruction. These tasks are demonstrated using standard glyph selection for complete family synthesis to show advantages compared with reference techniques.

We propose a framework designed to theoretically analyze ensembles comprising low-complexity expected risk minimizers, trained on independent random compressed versions of high-dimensional data. Our contribution begins by defining a general, distribution-specific upper limit on excess risk formulated through a specific definition of compressibility. This intrinsic bound operates independently of the input data's dimensionality while illuminating the internal regularization mechanisms inherent in compression-based techniques. Next, we apply this general bound to both regression and classification tasks by utilizing Johnson-Lindenstrauss mappings as our chosen compression architecture. For each specific application, our approach involves constructing a tight upper limit on the compressibility function, thereby revealing geometrically based distributional requirements under which compressive strategies achieve minimax-optimal performance rates, modulo polylogarithmic overheads. Specifically, compressive classification attains these rates subject only to a mild geometric margin condition and a flexible moment condition that generalizes significantly beyond the restriction to bounded domains. Furthermore, in the context of regression with strongly convex and differentiable loss functions, compressed regression effectively harnesses spectral decay, offering results that are essentially near-optimal. Central to deriving this primary upper bound is a high-probability uniform limit on integrated deviations for dependent empirical processes, an element that holds potential for independent interest.

The emergence of various wireless technologies has necessitated the development of 6G networking systems that integrate sense, compute, and communicate (ISCC) capabilities over shared spectrums. To support this, we offer a cohesive framework designed to maximize limited resources within ISCC ecosystems. Specifically, we derive two distinct dual-beamforming design strategies grounded in multi-objective optimization: one focused on maximizing total weighted performance and the other on minimizing aggregate transmit power. Extensive simulations confirm the viability of both approaches and further reveal parameter impacts that offer critical design insights for next-generation ISCC systems.

Although computer-aided diagnostics leveraging deep learning are increasingly employed to inspect analytical medical imagery, their practical utility in clinical settings remains limited by deficiencies in robustness and generalization; this challenge becomes particularly severe when historical training data is scarce. This study tackles such hurdles within a transfer learning framework, challenging the conventional wisdom of shifting knowledge solely from natural to medical image domains by demonstrating that training within the same domain yields significantly improved resilience and generalization capabilities. In light of this, we introduce a new two-tiered framework specifically designed for achieving universally generalized and robustness-enhancing medical image segmentation. Initially, an unsupervised autoencoder that learns from tile-based inputs is established to extract both localized insights and broader contextual representations. Subsequently, a segmentation model is coupled with an ancillary reconstruction network, which incentivizes the primary architecture to seize comprehensive semantic features. Extensive tests regarding lung segmentation across multiple chest X-ray datasets have produced results that confirm superior immunity to data corruption and outstanding adaptability to previously unseen datasets, notably even when constraints are imposed on the amount of available training data.

The Traveling Tournament Problem stands as a classic benchmark for scheduling sports leagues. This paper introduces an approximation algorithm specifically designed for TTP(2), a constrained variation limiting consecutive home or away games to at most two each for a tournament involving $n$ teams. Our proposed approach achieves an approximation ratio of $1 + 24/n$, establishing the inaugural approximation guarantee with an optimality ratio of $1 + O(1/n)$ for TTP(2).

This paper introduces a novel characterization method for binary cellular automata based on behavioral metrics evaluated against the simplified Boolean representation of their transition functions. Tailored by deriving heuristics from elementary cellular automata, these metrics classify patterns as either growth, reduction in scale, chaos, or stability. Utilizing these classifications yields two assessments of global behavior: first, a static measure that aggregates occurrences from the comprehensive truth table across all input combinations, and second, a dynamic measure representing the average behavioral outcome over multiple executions ($n$) generated by diverse initial random states. The study applies these assessments both to delineate an automaton's properties and to optimize the genetic algorithms' selection process, aiming to retrieve rule sets analogous to Conway's Game of Life. This approach enabled the discovery of a broad collection of sophisticated binary cellular automata exhibiting noteworthy traits, such as self-replication.

This study examines the discretization of an optimal stochastic control problem involving the parabolic differential equations, with both control variables included in diffusion. Through this study, convergence for this problem is established, even in situations where the input values contain errors; additionally, a Monte Carlo technique is proposed.

Few-shot image classification aims to identify novel categories utilizing only a restricted number of labeled examples. Previous research heavily focused on metric-learning strategies, wherein a target image is classified through the retrieval of the most similar prototype from an existing set, relying on feature distances. However, neural networks exhibit varying levels of confidence regarding the calculated similarities across different instance pairs. Accurately modeling and incorporating this uncertainty regarding similarities can enhance how efficiently limited data points are utilized during few-shot optimization. In response to this, our work introduces a new "Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot" framework that models probabilistic representations for query-support pair similarity and drives through uncertainty-optimized training procedures. By transforming observed distance measurements into probabilities and embedding them within the objective loss function, our approach achieves more robust optimization. to address the correlations among queries and support prototypes, a graphical model was adopted to estimate these uncertainties jointly. Comprehensive testing confirms that an extension over strong baselines and attains state-of-the-art accuracy.

We introduce a method to model the dynamic behavior of BCS superconductors using cold atoms confined within an optical cavity. By encoding effective Cooper pairs through the atoms' internal states and inducing attraction via the exchange of virtual photons among atoms linked to a shared cavity mode, this system allows us to manipulate interaction strengths. Combined with adjustable dispersion relations for these pairs, this capability enables the comprehensive investigation of the BCS model's dynamic phase diagram in response to system parameter variations and distinct initial states. This proposal offers a groundbreaking approach to exploring non-equilibrium characteristics of superconducting and magnetic quantum phenomena through the exploitation of atom-light couplings in cold atomic ensembles.

This article outlines an elementary yet effectively quantitative mathematical model designed to resolve the persistent lack of championships suffered by Canadian Hockey Teams. Utilizing Competitive Intransitivity as a practical framework of prediction, researchers demonstrate that when exclusively investing under a consistent salary cap in merely three independent variables (Offence, Defence, Goaltending), and having just three teams (e.g., Montreal, Boston, New York) apply distinct salary allocations, significant and counterintuitive shifts in gameplay results. This phenomenon mirrors rolling sets of intransitive dice across consecutive head–head matches. Most fundamentally, a hopeful implication emerges that every specific strategic path taken by one team inevitably exposes it to a counter-aesthetic approach by an opponent, all while remaining within identical financial constraints. Such a counter–strategic adaptation enables a clear pathway to victory in an additional playoff round, serving as a potential route beyond years of exclusion from the ultimate championship title.

Ultrawide bandgap (WBG) semiconductor technologies promise significant advancements in fast-emerging fields such as quantum communication, short-wavelength optometry, intelligent power generation, and biological interconnects. Although some aspects are realizable through traditional configurations, achieving superior performance and expanded functionality necessitates innovative hybrid system designs. We present a novel framework capitalizing on the intrinsic attributes of diamond $p$-n junctions integrated alongside electrical and optical manipulation of the depletion layer. By employing this junction as a transistor gate within the photo-switch structure, a working prototype for non-volatile operation in diamond has been established. A diamond $p$-n diote doped via nitogen for deep donors in the $n$-region exhibits visible light activation. Its intrinsic insulatory condition in the absence of illumination, characterized by an extremely low free-carrier density in the $n$-type gate, becomes pivotal when exposed; subsequent illumination restores effective conventional electrical gating to the transistor. Under dark conditions, the apparatus locks in ("is frozen"), maintaining permanent state memory, which introduces new paradigms for information and energy transmission with utility in aerospace electronics, avionics power systems, bioelectronic devices, and quantum networking contexts.

This study addresses recent crowd counting approaches utilizing the Plugging-and-Playing Patch Rescaling (PRM) module, specifically enhancing their capabilities for images characterized by perspective deformation, varying crowd density, extensive occlusion, and chaotic backgrounds. By maximizing the efficacy and potential of PRM technology, we developed a new Multi-Resolution Multi-Task (MRMT) network based PRM model. This architecture comprises three deep branches that generate distinct feature maps at varying resolutions, performing multi-level feature interleaving at a granular level to integrate vital collective information. Early-level features are also treated with visual mechanisms to enhance high-level branch capacities regarding the detection of prominent/primary regions. Our numerical analysis and visualization indicate that this model significantly outperforms its predecessor, PRM base approaches. This technique shows a 0% performance gain over existing state-of-the-art techniques on cross-domain benchmark evaluations.

Training robots in simulation using a wide range of controllers has allowed them to recover online from locomotion injuries. Nevertheless, discovering these diverse, high-quality controllers is difficult without specific hardware and hyperparameter tuning. Conversely, the Covariance Matrix Adaptation MAP-Annealing algorithm, a quality diversity technique based on evolution strategies, avoids these constraints and excels in benchmark environments yet suffers from quadratic scalability when handling modern neural networks. To address this, we apply ES-efficient approximations to create three scalable variants of CMA-MDE. Experimental results indicate our new methods exceed existing ES baselines in benchmark robots and rival state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning quality diversity approaches in benchmark tasks. Code and demos are provided at https://scalingcmamae.github.io.

Classifier robustness is a core element governing the dependability of Machine Learning (ML) systems, making assessment methods for this quality crucial. This study tackles the challenge of evaluating resistance to corruption in a manner that ensures both comparability and clarity across datasets. We introduce a data augmentation testing strategy anchored on a corruption distance parameter $\epsilon$, established by the innermost distance between distinct classes in the data. This leads to the MSCR metric, which calculates mean statistical corruption robustness and enables dataset-specific evaluations for contrasting classifiers. The MSCR figure is interpretable, signifying the accuracy loss that could theoretically have been avoided due to statistical noise. Examinations on both two-dimensional data and images demonstrate the metric mirrors variations in classifier solidity. Additionally, our analysis of models trained and tested at differing noise levels uncovers unforeseen performance peaks. Although a trade-off between standard accuracy and model robustness is commonly cited, our findings reinforce that this compromise is not an inevitable byproduct. Instead, our results show that applying basic data augmentation driven by robustness objectives can even marginally boost accuracy.

This paper introduces a method to infer room lighting conditions from a single indoor photograph using the proposed workflow: unlike previous attempts that rely either on overly simple models (lacking realism) or complex representations (difficultly editable for users afterwards). Instead this paper adopts a hybrid strategy combining both approaches: estimating a contempered set that includes parametric sources (allowing strong realistic shadows and easy editing) while integrating non parametric textures capturing high-frequency surfaces needed especially for rendering specular objects. The resulting predictions are therefore user editable, intuitive and interpretable allowing artist/users not only interpret them after several click modifications before they can also produce quantitative & visual competitive outcomes making it easier handle casual users. Results show how our framework accomplishes this goal by blending two existing techniques simultaneously.

Breathing oscillations in chiral antiferromagnetic skyrmions can be triggered by temporarily altering the strength of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction or magnetocrystalline anisotropy. Using an adiabatic approach, we derive a specific potential function that directly necessitates these breathing motions. By examining the nonlinear regime, we investigate characteristics associated with larger-amplitude oscillations, revealing a maximum amplitude threshold imposed by the potential. Consequently, we predict—and verify through numerical simulations—that large-scale breathing excites skyrmion annihilation. This annihilation process becomes efficient even when the skyrmion is only mildly initially perturbed, causing its radius to expand before internal breathing dynamics ultimately destroy it. Intriguingly, we demonstrate that skyrmions maintain nonzero kinetic energy precisely at the moment of disappearance. Furthermore, we establish the frequency for small-amplitude breathing oscillations.

Reliable, safe, and punctuated operation of cyber-physical systems—from avionics parts to smart grids—requires careful management, especially given their inherent time-dependent dynamic nature and stochastic behaviors. Consequently, verification utilities and modeling frameworks must be capable of handling these specific quantitative features. In an invitation to contribute to a presentation delivered at the 2022 Modeling Abstractions in Real Systems workshop (MARS), the paper provides insights on quantitative model verification using the Modeled formal language and associated Modeless Toolset through exploration of recent investigations and escalating needs in expressivity and computational power. The first case addresses power supply noise in a Network-wide-on-Chip model, represented by a Markovian chain; second, it examines signal flow within satellite nodes via Markov decision processes employing diffusion-based intelligence; finally the third case investigates Bitcoin attack strategies using advanced modeling methods for Markovian Automata.

In our paper, we build a hybrid mixed-radice number system over the generalized symmetric group $G(m, 1,n)$, also known as a complex reflection group. By developing a subexceedance functional associated with this group, we also establish a bijective mapping between the positive integers and group elements of $G(m, 1,n)$, alongside presenting an alternative enumerative system featuring a newly defined inversion statistic for $G(m, 1,n)$ elements.

We examine several facets of a cornerstone in quantum information theory: the Choi-Jamiolkowsky isomorphism [A. Jamiolkowsky, Rep. Math. Phys., 3, 275 (1972)]. Forecasting human pose is a difficult challenge due to the intricate nature of body movements and postures. In populated settings, an individual's motion can be significantly affected by the movements of others nearby. While previous attempts at multi-person dynamic pose forecasting often exist, many either treat the full pose sequence as a time series (neglecting connections between joints) or predict the future sequence only for a single person at a time. Addressing these constraints, this paper introduces Social Motion Transformer (SoMoFormer) for multi-person 3D pose forecasting. Unlike conventional transformers that process inputs along the time dimension, SoMoFormer's unique architecture models motion input based on joint sequences, enabling attention across individual joints during parallel predictions of entire future motions for each joint. With this reformulation of the problem, SoMoFormer effectively scales to multi-person environments via joint inputs from all individuals present. The system utilizes learned embeddings for joint type, person identity, and global location to capture inter-joint and inter-person relationships, allowing attention weights to increase for relevant nearby or related bodies. Evaluations show that SoMoFormer surpasses state-of-the-art approaches on benchmarks for long-term motion prediction, specifically the CMUT-MoCap, SoMoF, and MuPoTS-3D benchmarks. The objective of this study is to create a non-breath-held approach to myocardial T1 mapping that employs inversion-recovery (IR) radial rapid acquisition with relaxed constraints (FLASH) and a calibration-free reconstruction technique capable of handling motion. First, an analytical formula was developed to mitigate inversion wait time, accounting for incomplete tissue recovery to maintain calculation precision. Second, respiratory motion signals were extracted from the k-space center using modified adaptive singular value decomposition, known as SSA-FARY, based on evolving image contrast. Third, parameter maps and coil sensitivity estimates were directly derived from ordered k-space and temporal information through motion-aware regularization, allowing direct application of spatial total variation. Verification was conducted across a tissue-equivalent phantom, data from twenty-five healthy individuals, and a pig model of myocardial ischemia. Among findings, phantom data indicated excellent T1 accuracy compared to the reference IR spin-echo method even when the inversion interval was shortened from five to one second due to the developed formula. Furthermore, comparing the partial-four-parameter motion-aware regularization approach with other methods demonstrated improved image quality for dynamic myocardial sequences. The vast amount of code necessary for creating today's hardware systems frequently causes significant vulnerabilities to go unnoticed. Vulnerabilities posing specific risks to data confidentiality—particularly attacks on cryptographic keys and similar sensitive data—threaten the overall reliability of the systems affected. While formal techniques like information flow tracing are effective for detecting if data from sensitive sources moves to untrusted outputs or external modules, existing strategies typically depend on a rigid principle: that a target must receive zero influence from the source. Since adhering to this non-inference model is unrealistic for numerous applications, alternative approaches have been developed that instead calculate information exposure to filter out leakage deemed insignificant. Due to high computational cost, real-number quantification methods require approximation, which sometimes results in false negatives. To improve on existing methodologies, we reinterpret these approximations and present QFlow, a new automated analyzer that achieves a superior detection rate over earlier tools. Designed for ease of use, our tool enables even those without extensive expertise to pinpoint leakage pathways within digital hardware layouts, thereby aiding the creation of inherently more robust security designs.

Decades ago, Walter Kohn hypothesized that a semiconductor with no bandgap could become unstable if electron-hole pairs (known as excitons), bound by Coulomb forces, spontaneously formed. In this reconstructed ground state, a bandgap would emerge that disrupts the lattice symmetry—a direct outcome of electronic interactions. Current research demonstrates the existence of this excitonic insulator phase in zero-gap carbon nanotubes, utilizing many-body perturbation theory and quantum Monte Carlo simulations as rigorous computational validation. These calculations reveal a modulation of charge between the two carbon sublattices driven by excitonic order, which creates an observable bandgap. Remarkably, the gap size increases proportionally to the inverse of the tube's radius but shows only slight fluctuations in response to an applied axial magnetic field. These results challenge the conventional Luttinger liquid model applicable to carbon nanotubes while offering experimental strategies to distinguish between excitonic and Mott insulator states.

Following this, current research on participant selection is examined and categorized according to their respective methodologies. The paper ultimately outlines pivotal future research avenues for these mechanisms, grounded in a critical analysis of the field's cutting-edge developments.

Human interaction with conversational agents happens frequently, a trend driven by the rapid evolution of neural networks in generative language modeling that have enhanced the creation of these agents. Although research commonly assesses model output via crowdsourced feedback, no established guidelines exist for conducting such evaluations, and it remains unclear whether cognitive biases among worker participants skew these judgments. Furthermore, external variables such as the time elapsed and prior task familiarity significantly influence consistency in inter-judging.

Cross-sectional predictions are ubiquitous, particularly in healthcare when forecasting outcomes via electronic health records across diverse patient populations. This work concentrates on constructing rigorous valid prediction intervals (PIs) for time series regression problems featuring cross-sectional data. A PI is defined as valid when it encapsulates the actual response variable with a high pre-established probability, and we distinguish between cross-sectional and longitudinal notions of validity. Cross-sectional validation applies across the diverse sample of time series, whereas longitudinal validity addresses the temporal component. Although ensuring coverage across both dimensions would be optimal, we demonstrate that distribution-free temporal (longitudinal) validity cannot be theoretically guaranteed. To address this, we introduce Conformal Prediction with Temporal Dependence (CPTD), a method that ensures guaranteed cross-sectional validity while mitigting the temporal dimension. CPTD serves as a versatile, lightweight post-hoc technique compatible with existing models, provided a calibration set is accessible. With an emphasis on neural networks due to their proficiency in capturing complex relationships within data such as diagnosis codes, extensive experiments verify that CPTD surpasses baseline methods across various datasets by enhancing longitudinal coverage and often producing tighter, more efficient prediction intervals.

Developing Video Question Answering (VideoQA) systems is critical to support humans in daily operations by retrieving answers from long-duration videos containing diverse and intricate events. While current multi-modal VQA models demonstrate strong performance on static images or short clips—particularly thanks to recent advancements in large-scale multimodal pre-training—they face novel obstacles when applied to long-form videos. Dense sampling approaches are computationally unfeasible, whereas sparse sampling methods falter when scenarios demand reasoning across multiple events and at varied levels of granularity. This study proposes Multi-modal Iterative Spatial-temporal Transformer (MIST), a novel architecture designed to enhance pretrained models' suitability for long-form VideoQA. MIST reconfigures traditional dense spatial-temporal self-attention into a cascaded system of segment and region selection modules that adaptively identify question-relevant frames and visual areas, allowing for efficient processing of visual details across different grains via subsequent attention mechanisms. Furthermore, MIST performs iterative selections and attention operations over multiple layers to facilitate multi-event reasoning. Exmissions evaluated across four benchmark datasets (AGOQA, NExT-QA, STAR, and Env-QA), along side recent achievements, show that MIST reaches peak results and shows state-of-the-art performance with improved computational power and depth.

This study introduces a new motion segmentation technique named LAAV (Locally Affine Atom Voting), whose primary innovation relies on utilizing sets of features to determine segmentation rather than the individual features of every element in the scene. Serving as a preprocessing step for image features, LAAV is subsequently integrated with an optimized variant of the leading state-of-the-art Random Voting (RV) method. Distinguishing itself from traditional approaches, LAAV employs feature-set affinities instead of pairwise affinities between all features; this strategy drastically simplifies complex situations, decreases computational burden, and maintains accuracy without degradation. We detail how LAAV overcomes the difficulties previously hampered older methods and evaluate our algorithms alongside other current benchmarks, demonstrating that it delivers the highest motion segmentation accuracy and achieves comparable performance to rival approaches even when measurement noise is present.

This work presents a newly developed finite volume approach utilizing unstructured mesh-vertex grids to model coupled solute transport and shallow water systems over complex terrain. We introduce innovative, well-balanced discretization schemes capable of maintaining positivity for both pollutant concentrations and free-water surfaces. The hydrodynamic component is designed to preserve water height non-deligibility, ensuring the positivity necessary when solving for steady, liquid-at-rest lake models, whereas diffusion transport guarantees maintaining positivity throughout. These methods also maintain the solutary concentration perfectly for any fluid domain except when considering topographical variations in source-terms. Of key interest, this novel numerical reconstructive model for solutary concentration and surface levels allows a violation of discrete minimum-maximum principles regarding maximal or minimal constants. To assess precision and ensure performance characteristics of these systems under varying conditions, this study utilizes a suite of simulation-based demonstrations. These evaluations confirm the accuracy, well-balanced states, and inherent advantages these numerical methods impart in solving coupled steady-state transport and water level dynamics equations.

Deep Neural Network variants are commonly utilized to construct parametric projections of spoken word segments with variable durations into fixed-dimensional vector representations, known as Acoustic Word Embeddings (AWEs). Yet, there is ambiguity regarding the reliability AWE distance measurements offer in estimating word-form resemblance. This study addresses whether acoustic embedding distance aligns with phonological difference by empirically evaluating various supervised architectures and training objectives for generating AWES. We trained embedding models for controlled German-Czech settings and assessed them on word distinguishment and phonological similarity tasks, revealing two key insights: best-case ACWE distance modulationally associates with phonological distance; enhancing word distinguishment does not inherently improve phonological similarity alignment. We advocate to reconsider standard ACUE intrinsic evaluation metrics for future research.

We demonstrate that systematic full configuration-interaction (FCI) calculations effectively predict the energy spectra along with the intrinsic spatial and spin structures of the many-body wavefunctions as the detuning parameter varies, focusing on three-electron hybrid qubits derived from GaAs asymmetric double quantum dots. Notably, while weak interaction scenarios typically treat the three-electron double-dot system as a single integral unit, this FCI approach highlights that enhanced charge interactions generate distinct spectroscopic patterns characterized by the emergence of Wigner molecules (WMs). Evidence of such molecular formation includes a significant reduction in energy gaps relative to non-interacting electron models and the occurrence of two-avoided-crossing events between states corresponding to twosome occupations of the left and right quantum dots. Physically, this entailed strong localization within individual wells; a phenomenon invisible to earlier theoretical frameworks based on independent-particle or two-site-Hubbard approximations employed in hybrid qubit modeling. We deep-dive into the conditions favoring strong WMs using a suite of modified FCI diagnostics—including charge and spin density plots and conditional probability distributions—and also compute energy spectral variations against increasing Coulomb repulsion (holding detuning constant) to further elucidates the drivers of WM emergence. Our findings show outstanding congruency with recent experimental results. Moreover, this FCI strategy, suitable for multi-well quantum dots, allows for immediate application to valleytronic Si/SiGe hybrid qubits operating within two bands, a system where the critical importance of WM dynamics was just validated experimentally.

This study presents the inaugural detection of the cyanomethyl molecule, CH$_2$CN, within a protoplanetary disk. As Embodied AI advances, agents are increasingly required to handle complex interactions within their environment. While existing tasks, such as Embodied Referring Expression and other question-and-answer tasks, predominantly focus on linguistic instruction, enabling agents to actively manipulate physical objects presents a significant challenge. To address this, we propose a novel task: Remote Embodied Manipulation Question Answering (REMQA), which integrates Embodied Referring Expression with active manipulation. In the REMQA setting, an agent must navigate to a remote location to operate on a target object to answer a query specifically designed around that action. We constructed a benchmark dataset for this new task using the AI2-THOR simulator. Additionally, we introduced an architecture featuring three-dimensional semantic reconstruction combined with a modular network design to tackle these challenges. Final evaluations on our custom REMQA dataset demonstrate the proposed framework's efficacy.

Smart contracts enable the definition of interaction protocols between entities lacking mutual trust by translating natural language terms into the executable code inherent in the system. Although representing contracts on a blockchain offers theoretical seamless integration, their effectiveness critically depends on the accuracy of input data—specifically timestamps. This study investigates, empirically, the deviation between intended contract outcomes based on precise timing versus what results occur amidst blockchain inaccuracies. We introduce a novel performance metric known as "execution accuracy," which evaluates this alignment, particularly focused on smart contracts with specific time-interval dependencies where logical behavior dictates whether execution happens inside or outside a designated window. Testing was conducted across local Ganache development environments alongside the Quorum network and public Ethereum testnet chains, Rinkeby and Görli. Results support our hypothesis that logic becomes increasingly unreliable as interaction timestamps approach defined boundaries, directly impacting confidence. One- and two-dimensional integrable quantum field theories belong to a rare and restricted class where calculating physically observable quantities yields explicit, closed forms due to the S-matrix factors governing their scattering interactions. Specifically, these models express correlation functions as exact series of multiple integrals valid non-perturbatively across any strength of the coupling constant. However, determining the convergence of these series and consequently the mathematical rigor of the resulting correlation operators remain largely unresolved challenges. This paper outlines the frameworks for such theories and details recent advancements concerning convergence proofs within these models specifically for the 1+1 dimensional massive Sinh-Gordon quantum field model.

Despite recent progress, achieving syntactic generalization in text decoders remains difficult. Furthermore, we achieve equal or superior results on conventional machine translation benchmarks. Additional quality assessments highlight scenarios where standard transformer models fail to capture syntactic nuance effectively, illustrating that embedding such structural information offers a tangible advantage.

This research aims to refine the initial reference trajectory using a continuous optimization method designed to navigate Multi-rotor Aerial Vehicles through unknown environments while ensuring clearance from obstacles. The system utilizes a dual-planning architecture consisting of global and local components. The global planner modifies the initial trajectory whenever it intersects with obstacles or passes dangerously close to one, delegating the calculation of the near-optimal control strategy to the local planner. The global planning stage incorporates two convex programming strategies: a primary method for trajectory refinement and a fallback method for trajectory recovery if refinement proves unsuccessful. The system prioritizes real-time performance and effective obstacle avoidance through these strategies. To support safety, dynamic feasibility, and accurate low-speed reference trajectory tracking, we formulated the local planning algorithm based on constrained nonlinear model predictive control, with the provision that the planners operate at mean computational speeds of 0.06s (15Hz) and 0.05s (20Hz) respectively on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX device. Our results confirm that within cluttered environments, this approach surpasses three other solutions: sampling-based pathfinding followed by trajectory generation, standalone local planning, and graph-based pathfinding followed by trajectory generation.

This study introduces a new strategy for classifying sentiments in multilingual short texts. Unlike previous methods that depend on mapping inputs to English due to the scarcity of training data in non-English languages, our unsupervised approach eliminates this requirement by utilizing vast amounts of weakly labeled multilingual data. By implementing a multi-layer convolutional network and pre-training it across various languages—demonstrated as critical to its success—we achieved state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks, notably excelling in recent SemEval-2016 Task 4 evaluations on several languages. Additionally, the outcomes of a single-language model trainer versus one trained jointly on all languages compare closely; while the unified model experiences marginally reduced accuracy, it significantly enhances generalization across different languages despite maintaining acceptable performance levels.

We analyze a first-order approach describing the joint development of a quantum scalar field and a classical Friedmann universe. Our approach captures a fully consistent, semi-classical evolution that inherently includes non-perturbative backreaction arising from particle generation. When examining these findings against a standard model lacking such dynamics—effectively a quantum field in fixed spacetime or one with adiabatic expansion applied perturbatively—we find the non-perturbative approach consistently modifies particle creation and alters cosmic expansion, yet confirms all such effects remain effectively trapped.

This work examines low-degree polynomial functions defined on the inner products of a set of stochastic vectors. Although the influence of relativity on electronic density has been extensively researched prior to our study, its impact on the pair probability, intracule density, and extracule density has yet to be examined previously. The advancement of ground and space-based telescopes depends critically on innovation in wavefront sensing and control technology. Achieving diffraction-limit observatories capable of countering Earth-atmospheric turbulence, as well as space instruments managing optical aberrations and telescope jitter, relies on novel technologies and unconventional concepts. Several established frameworks allow for wavefront decomposition, including modal Zernike coefficients, Fourier bases, and zonal modes. Yet to date, methods centered solely on these mathematical constructs have overlooked a paramount factor in astronomical optics: the human capital involved. This document proposes a new decomposition model termed the "Many-Headed Hydra" Modal Basis, wherein individual adaptive optiques community members are represented as functional modal heads to facilitate wavefront analysis. Testing reveals that the first author functions as an optimal decomposition model and achieves reconstruction accuracy resembling a correction within roughly 1% of the original turbulent field. We outline the resulting implications for deformable mirrors, closed-loop AO/active control strategies, and new horizons for predictive control. Underlying this investigation is the hypothesis that the first author's efficacy in this model foreshadows their prospective success in high contrast imaging.

Pedestrian localization and classification have garnered significant attention because of their broad utility in fields like security and autonomous driving. Despite recent advancements in pedestrian detection, performance remains constrained by fixed Intersection over Union (IoU)-based assignment and regression strategies. This limitation arises from two critical issues: first, IoU thresholds face a trade-off where lower settings generate more false positives and higher settings discard matched positives; second, IoU-based ground-truth-to-proposal assignment suffers from inconsistent supervision, causing spatially adjacent yet similar proposals to match different ground-truth boxes, leading conflicting regression directions for the model. This study highlights the profound impact regression direction detection performance has on pedestrian localization. To mitigate IoU deficiencies, we propose a geometrically sensitive search algorithm serving as an alternative assignment and regression metric. Unlike the conventional \textbf{one-to-one} IoU matching paradigm, our approach fosters more effective correspondences between sets of proposals and ground-truth bounding boxes. Evaluated on the CityPersons dataset, our method achieves higher MR-FP scores at R\_75, and integrating it into state-of-the-art detectors yields consistent performance gains across the board.

This research examines Wigner crystallization within phosphorene quantum dots, which feature electrostatic confinement in both circular and elongated geometries. Due to the effective mass anisotropy, Wigner molecules can form even when the ground state's charge density symmetry ranks lower than the confinement potential. In circular quantum dots, single-electron islands emerge for systems with four or two electrons but fail to appear with only three. The spectral fingerprints associated with Wigner crystallization are analyzed for potential resolution through transport spectroscopy. A hallmark of systems hosting these Wigner molecule states comprises a nearly degenerate zero-magnetic-field ground state ($B=0$) and high sensitivity to magnetic field-induced spin polarization. Conversely, in electron configurations lacking distinct single-electron island formation, $B=0$ excited states exhibit more degeneracy; furthermore, the confined system displays ground state symmetry transitions at magnetic fields roughly equalling 1 Tesla. The five-electron system within a circular quantum dot emerges as a distinct special case, exhibiting dual charge configurations dependent on the magnetic field. The first configuration involves formed single-electron islands in the lab frame, representing a zero-point ground state akin to that observed in three-electron pair-correlation functions. The second shows no such islands. In parallel, quasi-one-dimensional Wigner molecule formation proves more probable when elongated dots align along their zigzag direction, which supports the heavier electron mass parallel to that axis. Meanwhile, the lower effective mass parallel to the armchair axis facilitates the quantum "freezing" (imprisonment/reduction) of the electrons' transverse kinetic degrees of freedom.

Over the last ten years, the causal inference field has adopted various weighting techniques designed around precise covariate balance. These exact methods mitigate the dangers of extreme sample weights and model errors inherent in inverse probability weighting, but they eliminate all imbalance only by solving strict optimization constraints that often fail when groups exhibit poor overlap or when variables number in thousands. To address these feasibility hurdles, recent approximate balancing methods employ flexible inequality moment constraints rather than strict ones. Nevertheless, practitioners face difficulty choosing threshold parameters as the constraint count increases, and moment constraints do not always fully characterize the gap in covariate distributions. We introduce a new approach termed Mahalanobis balancing, which achieves balance across distributions from a multivariate stance. By utilizing a quadratic constraint governed by a single threshold that admits a straightforward selection process, we effectively control overall imbalance. We demonstrate that Mahalanobis bounding problem has an equivalent regularized l_1 norm regression setup and clarify its relationship to propensity score modeling, subsequently extending this methodology to include high-dimensional data contexts. Finally, we conduct rigorous numerical experiments evaluating its asymptotic behavior alongside its comparison to established balancing strategies.

Selecting the appropriate model and estimating its parameters from experimental fittings are foundational steps in biomechanics. Decades of computationally intensive hemodynamic research have heavily relied on decades-old constitutive equations for shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluids developed by Bird, Carreau, Cross, and Yasuda. The current work returns attention to these formulations primarily to resolve ambiguities in naming conventions and to tackle the critical issue of inferring parameters from rheological measurements. Through both re-analysis of published datasets and computer simulations, this study reveals extensive, nearly flat regions in the likelihood landscape. Consequently, this results in distinct sets of parameters that perfectly fit experimental observations yet predict markedly different flow behaviors. Because such variations can be used to draw erroneous physical inferences—even about metrics like zero-shear viscosity or relaxation times—the findings suggest these specific parameters lack predictive reliability. Finally, it was confirmed that this inherent limitation in parameter identifiability arises from the model's structure itself, not the data, as synthetic datasets featuring similar non-concentric results demonstrated this issue persists even against simulated inputs.

A Bose polaron typically denotes an impurity within a Bose-Einstein condensate. For dilute systems, the polaron's characteristics are presumed to be universal, governed solely by limited parameters defining the interactions between impurities and bosons; specifically, under weak interaction regimes, these properties rely exclusively on the scattering length associated with these contacts. This study, an expansion preceding references to previous findings in Ref. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 123403 (2021)], analyzes stronger boson-impurity couplings with finite range limits. Our findings indicate that even for attractive impurity-boson interactions up through the unitary limit, the entire set of static properties of a dilute Bose polarons can be determined using the scattering length alongside a supplementary metric characterizing the interaction's finite range. This methodology holds validity when such a supplementary metric diverges minimally from the scattering length regarding internal boson interactions, with a rigorous boundary provided in the work. Furthermore, we derive clear formulae for polaron energy and other attributes when impurity-boson interactions are tuned to unitarity, along with delivering the initial correction terms for deviations from this specific condition.

As mathematical models simulating cellular cardiac action potentials have advanced, gaining sophistication particularly in the gating kinetics that regulate ion channel openings and closures, understanding the hidden uncertainty within parameter calibration estimates becomes crucial, as does a methodological shift towards personalized medicine for clinical insights. This work employs approximate Bayesian computation to re-evaluate the gating kinetics across four specific ion channels in two pre-existing human atrial cell models using their original datasets, thereby quantifying parameter uncertainty and highlighting the pitfalls of relying on single unique values based solely on existing experimental evidence. The study examines two strategies for reducing such uncertainty: utilizing more comprehensive datasets and adopting a streamlined model formulation requiring fewer parameters to constrain the system. Upon integrating the re-configured models back into the full simulation to assess the impact on action potentials, it is observed that while employing expanded datasets does not resolve existing estimation uncertainties, adopting a less complex model—specifically regarding the fast sodium current—delivers an improved fit to experimental data, reduces parametric uncertainty, and enhances computational efficiency.

This paper introduces B-tree enhancements tailored for contemporary storage hardware featuring transparent inline compression. While recent discourse has favored log-structured merged (LSM-trees) as B-tree replacements—citing benefits in storage density and write efficiency—this work advocates for reconsidering this view given the advent of built-in hardware compression. Modern appliances like all-flash arrays and next-generation compute/storage drives offer lossless compression transparent to the OS and apps, potentially mitigating physical cost gaps between LSM and B-tree structures. Furthermore, these innovations open avenues to reduce B-tree write amplification. As an initial investigation, the paper outlines three techniques—deterministic page shadowing, localized page modification logging, and sparse redo logging—to significantly curb write amplification using these compression-capable drives. Experiments executed on a commercial drive with transparent compression reveal that these designs slash B-tree write amplification by over 10x. When pitted against RocksDB, a standard LSM-based key-value store, the optimized B-tree demonstrates equivalent or lower write amplification and storage footprint.

Recent progress in transfer learning and the pre-training of large contextualized models has accelerated innovation across various real-world domains, including dialogue assistants. This paper investigates the generalized zero-shot setup for intent recognition based on a sentence pair modeling technique aligned with standard best-practices for zero-shot text classification. The proposed method achieves SOTA F1-score improvements of up to 16% on unseen intent categories and an additional 7% through lexicalizing the intent labels; notably, these results are reached by utilizing only intent labels and user utterances, requiring no external knowledge sources. Furthermore, leveraging task transfer from other sentence pair tasks, such as Natural Language Inference (NLI), facilitates additional performance gains.

**Summary:** Advances in precision medicine, biodiversity research (bioscience), and synthetic biology require more sophisticated modeling approaches. The Simulation Experiment Description Markup Language (SED-ML) was created as a community-driven, standardized format to enable collaborative simulation work, but its effectiveness is currently limited by weak software support and inconsistent interpretations of the standard across platforms. To resolve these issues and enforce consistent Sed-ML usage, we developed validation software that assists researchers in debugging their simulations and promoting interoperability. We applied this validator to fix errors in official SED-ML examples and plan to update records in the BioModels database to improve simulation compatibility. We expect this validator will significantly enhance simulation prediction accuracy while driving broader adoption and standard compliance within the scientific community to address the complex challenges of biosimulation and synthetic medicine through a universally accepted approach.  

**Availability**: Access to our validator tool begins as a free service through three platforms - the public RESTful Web Form, direct HTTP interface, command-line utility, and open-source (BSD) licensing Python package. The source code is open source, available on GitHub repositories. The tool currently includes integration into 11 different simulation software packages.

This study introduces a search for generic short-duration gravitational wave (GW) bursts within data collected during the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo. We employ a coherent WaveBust (cWB) algorithm improved by a decision-tree classification machine learning model designed to separate GW signals from noise transients more effectively. This machine learning component, capable of detecting stochastic signals uncorrelated to any known signal model despite training on representative noise, maintains the search’s independence from specific signal models. We demonstrate that the machine-enhanced cWB pipeline offers detection capabilities at greater distances compared to earlier model-independent methods. Sensitivity gains, reaching near order-of- magnitude improvements in detectable amplitudes while reducing the alarm threshold frequency to one per century, are achieved across various simulated signal spectra. Although efficient in applications like motion capture and sport analysis, and offering robustness to single-view inconsistencies, multi-view 3D human mesh estimation has received minimal research focus. Comprehensive evaluations confirm the method's significant enhancements in scenarios involving previously unseen outdoor scenes compared with prior approaches.
