We examine the PAC learning of noisy quantum stabilizer states by utilizing Aaronson's (2007) PAC framework for quantum states. Although an algorithm for noiseless quantum state learning was introduced by Rocchetto (2018), a solution for noisy scenarios remained unresolved. Drawing on classical learning theory's methods for noise robustness, we define a Statistical Query (SQ) model for quantum state PAC learning and demonstrate its resilience to typical noise types, such as classification and depolarization noise in the SQ context. Additionally, we establish an exponential lower bound for learning stabilizer states using the SQ model. Furthermore, we provide evidence outside the SQ framework that, in the presence of noise, learning stabilizer states is generally as complex as the classical Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem; consequently, we position the learning of quantum states as the quantum equivalent of classical learning with parities—solvable when noiseless but appearing computationally impossible even with elementary noise forms.

This paper introduces NNCF (Neural Network Compression Framework), a new architecture for optimizing neural networks via post-compression fine-tuning. By adopting recent techniques like binaryization, quantization, and sparsity, NNCF generates hardware-optimized models capable of running efficiently across dedicated AI accelerators and general-purpose CPUs or GPUs without sacrificing inference latency or maintaining baseline accuracy for a broad array of architectures. Users can utilize either the provided annotated datasets through the tool as part of a standalone integration package designed to fit seamlessly into current training workflows. Available as part of OpenVINO Training Extensions, a Windows-compatible version hosted at github can now be installed via Pytorch.

This study utilizes the COSMOS2020 catalogues to investigate the stellar-to-halo mass relation ($M_*/M_h$) for central and satellite galaxies spanning a redshift range from 0.2 to 5.5. Following reliable photometric redshifts determinations to measure the near-infrared-selected two-point angular correlation and stellar mass functions across ten specific redshift bins, we constrain parameters with an HOD-based modeling approach. For each redshift, we calculate the $M_*/M_h$ ratio, revealing a dependence on halo mass that peaks near $M_h^{\rm peak} \sim 10^{12}\, M_{\odot}$, supporting the hypothesis of increasing halo mass at higher peaks for star-formation efficiency as redshift rises. Furthermore, we examine satellite prevalence relative to stellar mass and redshift, finding that satellite fraction declines across all stellar mass limits with increasing redshift, yet low-mass satellites comprise a higher proportion at fixed redshifts. The satellites contribute more significantly than centrals to total halo stellar mass budgets when halos exceed $10^{13}\, M_{\odot}$, yet remain consistently below the observed peak, suggesting active quenching processes in massive halos suppress stellar formation efficiency. Additionally, we assessed these findings against three hydrodynamic simulations—Horizon-AGN, Illustris-TNG-100, and EAGLE. The largest divergence lies at the high-mass extreme, where simulated satellite contributions generally exceed observational data, including elevated overall satellite populations. Both observations point to potentially inefficient mass-assembling feedback mechanisms in group and cluster-sized halos within the simulations compared to reality, or suggest a later quench timelines for accreting mass in such runs.

We present a Bayesian methodology designed to forecast continuous or categorical outcomes utilizing data from multisourced inputs organized into a multi-dimensional tensor framework. Illustrated through a motivating study on molecular predictors of early-life iron deficiency (ID) derived from several 'omics datasets spanning various developmental timepoints in a rhesus macaque model, the approach employs a linear framework. This framework incorporates low-rank structures within the coefficients to account for multi-way dependencies while distinguishing coefficient variance across sources to assess relative importance. The utilization of conjugate priors enables computationally efficient Gibbs sampling for posterior estimation, applicable to continuous normal outcomes as well as binary outcomes connected via a probit link. Simulation experiments confirm that the model yields expected performance regarding coefficient correlation accuracy and prediction error rates, notably improving upon standard models by leveraging structured interactions and adjusting for varying signal intensities per source, ultimately demonstrating effective classification in our applied scenario. The corresponding R software package is accessible at https://github.com/BiostatsKim/BayesMSMW.

Weakly-supervised learning (WSL) has been suggested to reconcile the trade-off between labeling costs and model accuracy using sparse annotations—such as single points, bounding boxes, or scratches—and has demonstrated significant success, especially within image segmentation. Nevertheless, this challenge remains due to restricted supervision, particularly in scenarios involving minimal labeled data. Furthermore, nearly all current WSL segmentation techniques target star-shaped objects, which differ substantially from curvilinear entities like blood vessels or nerves. This paper introduces YoloCurvSeg, a framework leveraging image synthesis to address sparse annotation needs in curvilinear structures, based solely on image inpainting for dilated skeletons to generate backgrounds matching real data distributions. These are combined with randomly simulated curves, created by a foreground generator utilizing the Space Colonization Algorithm, and synthesized through contrastive patch-wise learning to produce synthetic data containing both images and segmentation labels, requiring input from merely one to a few noisy skeleton labels. Finally, a segmenter is trained on this synthetic data alongside potentially available unlabeled data. Evaluated across four open datasets (OCTA500, CORN, DRIVE, and CHAME_DB1), YoloCurvSeg surpasses leading WSL segmentation methods significantly, securing over 97% of fully-supervised performance with only one noisy skeleton annotation (accounting for 0.14% to 1.40% depending on the dataset compared to full annotations). The project resources, code and datasets, are hosted online at https://github.com/ZeyuanLi/YoloCurvSeg.

Effective for speech translation, speech segmentation divides lengthy audio into manageable clips. Furthermore, the authors developed a hybrid approach that integrates these classification models with VAD. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this new method significantly surpasses conventional segmentation in the performance of both cascaded and end-to-end translation architectures.\

The existence of spin\textsuperscript{$C$}$^{}$ structures on all compact oriented 4-manifolds, a result established decades ago by Hopf and Hirzebruch, is often demonstrated via indirect and opaque proofs. This paper introduces a more direct and geometrically intuitive demonstration leveraging twistor spaces. Following an application of these concepts to illuminate diverse four-dimensional geometric phenomena, we illustrate how related methodologies extend the understanding of spin and spin\textsuperscript{$C$}$^{}$ structures to arbitrary dimensions.

In recent years, transformer architectures and their variations have excelled in numerous machine learning domains. This triumph is inherent to their ability to process long sequences and leverage attention-based, context-dependent weights. We contend that these features make transformers uniquely equipped for Meta-Reinforcement Learning. A meta-RL agent must identify tasks via trajectory sequences and employ rapid policy adaptation strategies, both achievable through the self-attention mechanism. In this study, we introduce TrMRL, a meta-RL system that replicates memory reinstatement through a transformer-based architecture. The model iteratively constructs episodic memory by linking recent working memory events across transformer layers via self-attention, generating a layer-by-layer consensus representation that minimizes Bayes Risk. The computed features then enable the derivation of optimal actions. Experiments conducted within high-dimensional continuous control realms, such as locomotion and fine motor manipulation, demonstrate that TrMRL matches or surpasses baselines in terms of sample efficiency, robustness to out-of-distribution tasks, and final asymptotic performance.

This study investigates the semiclassical properties of scattering data for non-self-adjoint Dirac operators featuring rapidly oscillating complex potentials that are analytic near the real axis. We offer many rigorous yet general proofs, whereas a full comprehension demands a concrete exploration of specific instances using WKB geometry. Relying on numerical findings originally published by Bronski and Miller over two decades ago, we conduct a thorough, rigorous uniform semiclassical analysis of the Bohr-Sommerfeld conditions for eigenvalue localization along analytic arcs and the related norming constants. These detailed calculations utilize a specific case studied numerically by said researchers for more than 20 years, incorporating the exact WKB approach. Conversely, regarding eigenvalues approaching zero and the associated reflection coeffient, we draw upon the extensive framework developed earlier by Olver. This work aims to elucidate the semiclassical dynamics of the focusing cubic NLS equation, which admits initial conditions of the form $A\exp\{iS/\epsilon\}$, leveraging the established insight by Zakharov and Shabat regarding how Dirac operator spectral analysis facilitates solving NLS equations via inverse scattering techniques.

This research investigates scattering in Dirac fermion fields against topological solitons arising from $(2+1)$-dimensional nonlinear $O(3)$ $\sigma$-model backgrounds using both computational and analytic techniques. Exact formulas characterizing the scattering are established, revealing symmetry features of partial wave amplitudes and $S$-matrix components. Within the Born approximation, the scattering matrix element expressions are analytically derived as well as the resulting differential and total cross-sections; their symmetrical behaviors and asymptotic characteristics are subsequently examined. Numerical approaches are employed to derive higher partial wave coefficients of the $S$-matrix in relation to fermion momentum, which leads to a detailed discussion and verification of the observed dependencies.

This work explores thermodynamic catalysis within the context of elementary thermal operations, leveraging this framework to elucidate catalytic dynamics. We introduce new technical instruments to facilitate the calculation of state transition rules, specifically providing a comprehensive characterization for qutrit systems. Applying these tools alongside numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the mere use of qubit catalysis significantly expands the range of accessible state transitions in qudit, substantially narrowing the divide between elementary thermal operations and general thermal processes. Furthermore, we analyze catalytic transitions by decomposing them into temporally resolved evolutions, allowing for the tracking of exchanges in nonequilibrium free energy. These findings provide evidence that catalysis in thermodynamics offers simple yet effective advantages, and they establish a robust method for examining how catalytic processes function.

Particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) is fundamentally applied in fluid dynamics to quantify three-dimensional time-resolved pressure and velocity components. However, localization errors during tracking remain a critical performance limiter for PTV, specifically within single-camera defocusing, plenoptic imaging, and digital in-lawe holography (DIH). To mitigate this, we introduced stochastic particle advection velocimetry (SPAV), a statistical objective function designed to enhance PTV precision. SPAV relies on an explicit particle advection framework to predict particle trajectories based on estimated velocities, allowing for the inclusion of non-ideal factors such as drag on inertial particles. The methodology derives and approximates the SPAV loss by comparing tracked versus advected positions while accommodating arbitrary tracking and localization uncertainties. Implemented via a physics-informed neural network (PINN), our simultaneous losses include both the SPAV statistic, a Navier-Stokes continuity term, and relevant wall boundary constraints. Validated on experimental and simulated DIH-PTV data featuring both turbulent and laminar regimes, the proposed statistical approach substantially surpasses conventional methods, yielding an average error decrease of approximately 50%. Additionally, this framework offers flexibility for integration with other data assimilation tools such as adjoint-variational strategies, Kalman filters, and observer-based techniques.

Ultra-cold atoms represent an ideal environment for interferometric experiments due to their macroscopic, coherent nature, which yields long coherence times and large lengths necessary for high-precision and high-sensitivity metrology. This review examines our attempts to enhance interferometer performance, highlighting the demonstration of a shortcut protocol for managing ultra-cold atoms in optical lattices compared to conventional methods. This shortcut strategy shrinks manipulation duration significantly by up to three orders of magnitude and facilitates the broader application of a matter-wave Ramsey interferometer to assess trapped motional quantum states. Using a shortcut-enabled echo sequence, we have extended system coherence by an additional order of magnitude while exploring multimode approaches to improve resolution. Specifically, the utilization of a robust multipath, multimode arrangement sharpens temporal fringe peaks through path multiplicity and achieves approximately double the resolution of a standard double-path two-mode setup, resulting in atomic momentum distributions narrower than 0.6 $\hbar k_l$, a feat further enabled by shortcut techniques for momentum resolution optimization. Moreover, employing principal component analysis (PCA), we devised strategies to discern and mitigate systematics, effectively lowering detection noise to nearly the $1/\sqrt{\hbar}$ quantum noise limit of a single photon while isolating and occasionally abolishing interference noise. These studies also yield a proposed scheme for precisely determining local gravitational acceleration over distances as short as centimeters using interferometric methods.

Meta-Reinforcement Learning (Meta-RL) transforms experience garnered across numerous tasks into a generalizable meta-policy that swiftly adapts—via minimal updates (sometimes just a single one)—to achieve near-ideal performance on comparable new challenges. We introduce EMRLD: using Demonstration (EMRLD) to address the scenario wherein only potentially non-ideal data or exhibits are accessible during training; this framework leverages such signals for effective guidance even when perfect examples remain unavailable by simultaneously exploiting Reinforcement Learning and supervised Learning across offline demonstrations with the ultimate aim of generating meta-policies showing consistent enhancements. We also propose EMRLD-WS, featuring warm start techniques tailored specifically towards datasets containing inefficient demonstration information, resulting in enhanced efficiency under constrained exploration conditions; furthermore we empirically validate that our EMRLD methods demonstrably surpass traditional alternatives within a broad selection of challenging sparse reward tasks like those involving autonomous navigation systems or mobile platforms exhibiting significant uncertainty.

Introducing a bump at similar low values of $Z$ and $\tau$ facilitates dust accumulation within vorticles that briefly exceed unit ratios, promoting SI onset prior to shear disruption and the subsequent formation of a turbulcnt, wide ring at $Z\approx0.01$. A significant focus of research involves analyzing large-scale neural population recordings in behaving animals with the goal of uncovering low-dimensional structures that facilitate interpretation. One established method for achieving this demixed Principal Component Analysis (dPCA), which uses supervised linear dimension reduction to isolate specific components tied to experimental conditions, is often utilized. In this study, I propose Kernel dPCA (kdPCA), a nonlinear adaptation of the original framework achieved by incorporating kernel least squares regression into the demixing process. Through simulations of neural activity structured at a lower dimensionality, I compare the components derived from both dPCA and kdPCA. These results indicate that linear demixing is disrupted when neural activity exhibits relevant nonlinear dynamics—such as rotations or stimulus-dependent gain—because these factors obscure components tied to individual experimental manipulations. Conversely, kdPCA successfully recovers these meaningfully interpretable elements even under such nonlinear conditions. Lastly, the efficacy of kdPCA is validated through applications to datasets from perceptual decision-making tasks featuring two distinct neural population recordings.

Recent breakthroughs in optical magnetometry now deliver unprecedented sensitivity across both macro and nano scales, a performance enhanced by wide bandwidth and operation outside cryogenic conditions that has already catalyzed numerous practical applications. However, we introduce an ambient-operating optical micro-magnetometer achieving the renowned picoTesla range for the first time, representing a gain of over three orders of magnitude compared to earlier work. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) plays a crucial role in investigating both the development and degeneration of brain white matter. However, established estimation protocols for DTI demand an extensive set of high-grade measurements, necessitating lengthy scan durations that are notably challenging for cooperative patient groups like infants. To address this limitation, this work introduces a novel approach capable of accurately deriving diffusion tensors using just six diffusion-weighted measurements. We accomplish this by training the model to capture interdependencies among diffusion signals and tensors within adjacent voxels. Leveraging transformer Networks—a state-of-the-art technique for modeling sequence relationships—our framework utilizes a dual-network architecture: the first network predicts diffusion tensors based on signal data from a neighborhood of voxels, while the second refines these predictions by further analyzing both the raw signal relationships and the initial tensor estimates across neighboring voxels. Validation across three datasets demonstrates that this method generates highly accurate diffusion tensor estimations, vastly outperforming three alternative methods. Furthermore, results derived from merely six measurements in our approach are comparable to those obtained via standard protocols requiring 30 to 88 measurements. Consequently, this technique holds the promise of reducing examination time for more dependable assessments of brain white matter in challenging populations, such as non-compliant neonates and young infants.

Battery energy storage serves a vital function within microgrids, where maintaining optimal battery operating temperatures is critical because excessive heat accelerates efficiency losses, shortens lifespan, and poses fire risks. Consequently, regulating the thermal profile of battery modules during operation is essential. Addressing this need, the proposed framework utilizes a two-layer control and operation strategy for integrated microgrid storage systems. Operating at two distinct levels, the first layer develops an optimal control policy to minimize fan speed and battery current requirements—thereby managing control efforts—so that a target temperature distribution is achieved within the modules. Building on this in the second layer, the microgrid operator calculates the ideal temperature distribution reference and battery current to minimize total system operational costs through optimal power flow analysis. With computational savings from this stratification, the approach supports the scalable deployment of battery systems. Simulation case studies are conducted to validate the proposed two-layer methodology's performance.

Background/foreground separation (BFS) involves isolating dynamic foreground objects from static scene elements and is a prevalent task in computer vision. This problem is typically addressed with standard cameras, leveraging their affordability, high resolution, and compatibility for human analysis. However, both these cameras and the algorithms used for data analysis struggle with common failure scenarios, including occlusions and drastic lighting changes, especially around highly reflective surfaces. Mitigating these limitations can be achieved by integrating another sensor modality for greater resilience. This research investigates whether an affordable radar system can effectively enhance the Robust PCA approach for BFS tasks. By utilizing emerging algorithm unrolling techniques, we achieve real-time computation, efficient feedforward inference, and robust generalization, outperforming conventional deep learning architectures. Benchmarked against the RaDICaL dataset, we demonstrate both the quantitative gains derived from including radar inputs and the qualitative robustness improvements, thereby alleviating typical failure points found in purely image-based methods.

Distributionally robust optimization employs multiple probability measures to define problem constraints, which can be aggregated into a risk functional that serves as a core component of distributionally robust stochastic programming. Multistage programming specifically demands conditional forms of these functionals to evaluate future risks following partial realizations and past decisions. This study outlines a methodology for constructing these conditional counterparts by mapping the inherent features of original risk functionals. It clarifies that the resulting conditionals are not equivalent to the nested analogues typically derived from lawInvariant measures and shows that combining both the initial measure and its nested decomposition enables practical applications in multistage stochastic distributionally robust frameworks.

While this approach mirrors models with fixed couplings proposed by others, this work extends it by incorporating time-dependent transition rates to better analyze their effects on critical phenomena. This occurs when the criticality parameters change, causing the destructive of the phase of radical absence and the elimination of radical agents over time in the population's steady states.

This research introduces a notion of VC-dimension tailored for subsets within groups. For a set \( A \), its definition relies on the VC-dimension of the family \(\{ (xA) \cap A : x \in A \cdot A^{-1} \}\). We establish that for finite subsets of an abelian group with this bounded VC-dimension, the convolution \( 1_A * 1_{-A} \) is demonstrably quantifiably stable under Bohr uniform continuity. This finding extends and robust aspects of a particular stable arithmetic regularity lemma developed by Terry and Wolfe across multiple dimensions. Specifically, our result directly validates that the Polynomial Bogolyubov–Ruzsa Conjecture—which represents a stringent form of the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa Conjecture—is true for collections exhibiting bounded classical VC-dimension; these foundational results remain valid within the context of non-abelian groups. Fundamentally, our contribution offers a structural theorem for translation-invariant families of subsets subject to stringent classical boundedness conditions. For translation-closed subsets within an abelian group having bounded classical VC-dimension, elements can be effectively characterized via Bohr sets.

The advancement of representation learning on user-item graphs for recommendation systems has shifted from utilizing single identifiers or interaction histories to leveraging higher-order neighborhood information. This shift catalyzed the success of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), such as PinSAGE and LightGCN. While effective, we contend that these models face two significant hurdles: (1) the overwhelming dominance of high-degree nodes distorts representation learning to the detriment of low-degree (long-tail) items, and (2) conventional representations remain sensitive to noisy interactions, as the aggregation mechanism inadvertently amplifies the weight of observed edges.

In this study, we investigate self-supervised learning applied to user-item graphs to enhance the accuracy and resilience of GCNs within the recommendation domain. Our strategy involves introducing an auxiliary self-supervised auxiliary task complementing traditional supervised recommendation learning to bolster node representations through self-discrimination. This approach entails generating diverse views of a node by applying operations like node dropout, edge dropout, or random walks to modify graph topology, with the objective of aligning different perspectives of the same node against divergent perspectives of others. Designated as Self-supervised Graph Learning (SGL) when adapted to state-of-the-art models like LightGCN, we theoretically demonstrate its ability to automatically extract harder negative samples. Empirical evaluations on three benchmark datasets substantiate that SGL enhances both recommendation precision—particularly for underrepresented items—and robustness against noisy user interactions. We introduce a simplified model for a domain wall within a thin ferromagnetic film. This wall is depicted as a nonreciprocal string, allowing transverse waves to travel at varying speeds depending on their direction. The system is defined by three specific parameters: mass density, tension, and a gyroscopic constant that measures the degree of nonreciprocity. Our analysis examines the distinctive behavior of nonreciprocal strings within bounded finite dimensions, demonstrating strong consistency with numerical simulations of ferromagnetic domain wall movement across strips of constant width.

The mystery of how the million-Kelvin corona can persist above the cooler photosphere remains an unresolved challenge in astrophysics that could potentially be unraveled through a detailed analysis of quiescent solar emissions, which occur independent of solar cycle phases. Although specific heating mechanisms in these regions are often too small-scale to observe individually, their properties emerge most effectively when studied statistically. This study introduces a refined, iterative refinement approach for determining heating characteristics using the empirical impulsive model defined by Pauluhn and Solanki. It adapts a  Machine Learning method previously specified in a published thesis to evaluate X-ray fluxes recorded by India's Chandrappha - 3. By applying this approach to X-ray measurements collected in various spectra—including those for 1–1.6 keV events—and correlating these frequencies with known patterns in our prior work, we estimate typical characteristic frequencies, amplitudes, periodicity distributions among affected areas within our current dataset. Observations reveal that these events produce roughly twenty-six observable bursts annually across all three studied spectral channels. These findings offer valuable new data detailing the characteristics and implications of sub-particle impulsive events necessary for understanding how quiet sunrays remain so distinctly cool despite the massive background corona.

Addressing the stereo-to-multichannel upmixing issue for music requires establishing the panning directions of instrument sources for rendering. We introduce an improved variational autoencoder that learns a latent space representing spatial acoustic images within multichannel mixes. Our approach separates spatial cues from auditory content, yielding latent variables independent of specific music tracks during inference where they guide source panning. We demonstrate this capability in two applications: transplanting the spatial layout of one recording to match another, and achieving automatic source control directly through the generative model. Objective metrics and listener experiments confirm that our method effectively isolates spatial imagery from audio content, facilitating transfer-based interactive audio rendering.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) hold significant promise for upcoming 6G wireless networks. However, scaling up RIS elements often introduces substantial overhead for channel acquisition and notable energy costs. Consequently, optimizing system capacity with fewer elements has become a critical challenge. Distinguishing itself from classical RIS structures, which rely on regular grid layouts for elements, this paper introduces an irregular RIS configuration. The fundamental concept involves asymmetrically deploying a fixed quantity of elements across a larger surface area. This arrangement grants augmented spatial degrees of freedom relative to regular designs, thereby boosting received signal power and elevating overall system capacity. We therefore define a joint optimization framework addressing both the network topology and precoding strategies to maximize capacity in irregular RIS-assisted systems. An efficient joint optimization algorithm is subsequently proposed, alternating between refining the irregular topology and the precoder design. Specifically, an irregular topology is generated using a Tabu Search-based approach, while a neighbor-extraction crossentropy algorithm handles the optimization of precoding weights. Empirical results indicate that, within the strict constraint of limited RIS elements, the proposed irregular design markedly improves system capacity.

Existing approaches typically consolidate frame-level visual features over time using methods like LSTM, Fisher Vectors, or NetVLAD to derive robust video representations. In this work, we propose a learnable aggregation strategy whose primary goal is to preserve the short-time temporal structure and spatial interdependencies found within frame-level features, alongside its adaptability to scenarios with extremely limited training data. Evaluation on a real-fake emotion recognition dataset highlights the method's superiority; it achieved a test MAP score of 65%, surpassing by only a mere single error the best-known Chalearn Challenge result of 66.7%. We anticipate that this framework is also suitable for future applications, including action or event recognition.

We introduce REDO, a class-agnostic framework capable of reconstructing dynamic objects from either RGB-D streams or calibrated videos. Unlike previous approaches, our problem setting balances increased realism and difficulty due to three main factors: (1) addressing cases where occlusion or imaging conditions obstruct partial visibility despite our goal of recovering the complete shape; (2) encompassing diverse object motions, such as non-deformation, deformable dynamics, and articulated movement; (3) enabling reconstruction of multiple object categories through a single unified system. To mitigate these hurdles, we present two innovative modules: first, a pixel-aligned canonical 4D implicit function that integrates accumulated temporal visual cues; second, a specialized 4D transformation module designed to capture object dynamics, thereby facilitating both temporal propagation and data aggregation. REDRO's performance was evaluated through extensive experiments across three databases: the synthetic SAIL-VOS 3D, the DeformingThings4D++ synthetic set for dynamic objects, and real-world 3DPW video. Results indicate that REDRO surpasses state-of-the-art dynamic reconstruction techniques by significant margins. Furthermore, ablation studies corroborate the necessity and effectiveness of each designed component.

Automatic accident recognition is a critical emerging field within traffic monitoring systems. With many modern urban crossroads now fitted with surveillance cameras integrated into traffic control networks, computer vision has emerged as an effective solution for automating this detection process. This paper introduces a robust and efficient architecture for monitoring intersection accidents. The methodology comprises a three-stage hierarchical pipeline: (1) deploying state-of-the-art YOLOv4 models for precise object detection; (2) maintaining object continuity through Kalman filtering combined with the Hungarian algorithm to resolve associations, utilizing an enhanced cost function that handles occlusions, overlapping items, and deformations; and (3) detecting collisions based on trajectory conflict analysis. These conflicts are identified by examining speed, direction, and proximity, encompassing scenarios such as vehicle-vs-vehicle, vehicle-vs-pedestrian, and vehicle-vs-cyclist. Tests on actual traffic footage demonstrate that the proposed system is viable for real-time deployment in surveillance settings, successfully distinguishing true traffic incidents and near-accidents at urban junctions with high recall rates and minimal false positives across varied lighting conditions evaluated via YouTube clips. The associated dataset, including these diverse video sequences from GitHub, facilitates access by researchers to support this open-access tool.

To address privacy concerns, multi-party gradient boosting methods have gained significant traction in machine learning research and practice, though few scalable, secure protocols exist for datasets partitioned across the horizontal. Two specialized HE-based protocols enable necessary non-linear calculations typical of tree boosting. Additionally, the framework details secure training and prediction mechanisms, supported by a formal analysis of its security and communication costs. Finally, experimental validation using two real-world datasets evaluates the framework's practical performance.

Ranking algorithms are vital for many online services, from search engines to recommendation platforms. This research reveals an unexpected phenomenon where popularity-driven sorting favors groups with fewer members that exhibit a specific signal: such small groups generate a disproportionately high share of total traffic compared to their numbers would suggest. Known as the "few-get-richer" effect, this occurs specifically in systems classifying items into distinct categories (like ideologically aligned news sources) when users prioritize top results and hold varied preferences across those categories. The authors provide analytical proofs of this occurrence under conditions featuring few classes combined with user preferences for specific groups and demonstrated click bias on prominent rankings. Computer simulations explore the conditions altering the strength of this phenomenon, which is further validated through controlled human experimentation. These conclusions hold significant implications for comprehending how misinformation propagates online.

Performance evaluations in a comparative listening test demonstrate that decomposition results from this method are of equal or superior quality compared to three other existing techniques. Significant gains are particularly visible in transient separation, where energy loss and unwanted leakage from other components are minimal, especially with signals dominated by pronounced transients. This study investigates cavitation within the context of the radial, isotropic displacement boundary value problem for compressible elasticity. The analysis focuses on a specific category of stored energy functions expressed as $W(F) + h(\det F)$, where $W$ behaves asymptotically like $||F||^n$ and $n$ represents the spatial dimension. Drawing on prior work by Vodopyanov, Goldshtein, and Reshetnyak regarding the properties of these functions, we establish that discontinuous deformations necessarily possess infinite energy. Furthermore, we characterize the exponential rate at which this energy increases. To resolve the issue where cavitating deformations otherwise lack finite energy, we propose a modified energy functional that incorporates a null Lagrange term identical to zero in the bulk. Crucially, energy minimizers for cavitating scenarios with finite total energy exist for this modified system.

The associated Euler–Lagrange equations mirror those of the original problem exactly at the interior; the distinction lies solely in the inner boundary conditions at the cavity. For the modified model, this condition mandates that a specific adjusted radial Cauchy stress function vanishes at the cavity surface. This vanishing condition effectively represents the divergence of the radial Cauchy stress to $-\infty$ originating in the unmodified formulation under the singular cavitating limit. This reformulation allows us to deduce several known variational results for finite-energy cavitating states under the new functional framework, including: 1) the existence of radial energy minimizers, 2) their adherence to Euler–Lagrange equations, 3) and the existence of a specific critical displacement value at the outer boundary that triggers cavitation. Additionally, we outline an iterative numerical strategy for computing these extreme solutions by analyzing smooth solutions defined over punctur ed domains, prove the scheme's convergence, present numerical findings—which include a simulation for inelastic limit cases—and ultimately suggest that our methodology is inspired largely by concepts borrowed from the renormalized energy theories applied to Ginzburg-Landau vortices.

The stability of disk galaxies and the origin of their anomalous rotation curves are critical test points for distinguishing between dark matter halo models and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We explore this using MOND simulations of the galaxy M33, running it in isolation for six billion years from the outset using an initial rotation curve (RC) match suitable for fitting the data. We found that lowering gas temperatures prevents the formation of excessive bars and bulges; despite the rapid development of a prominent bar in one year, it weakens considerably before matching observed characteristics, contrasting with the strong bars seen consistently in Newtonian simulations featuring dynamic dark matter. Consequently, the simulation yields a realistic 3 kpc corotation radius based on its pattern speed, yet the internal RC ascent remains overly rapid and velocity dispersions at the center are too elevated. Introducing a constant external acceleration approximating M30's gravity ($8.4 \times 10^{-12}\, m s^{-12}\, m^2$ at $30\degree$) slows the RC rise, inhibits material accretion at the galaxy core, and reduces central velocity dispersions. The overall outcome closely mimics several of M33’s key properties, demonstrating that even modest external fields significantly influence the evolution and structural integrity of disk galaxies. Future work must incorporate a temporally changing external field simulating M33’s complete galactic orbit to further verify its alignment with observations.

This study systematically analyzes synfire pulse train and firing rate propagation in an all-to-all coupled forward neuronal network. Differing from previous investigations that assumed solely reliable synaptic connections, this work principally explores how unreliable synapses affect these two activity types. The authors initially examine networks comprised entirely of excitatory neurons, demonstrating that both high-fidelity transmission probability and strong excitive drive greatly favor the transmission of neural activity, with network stability improving as these synaptic parameters are tuned effectively. Furthermore, the study reveals the noisy signals have varying but pronounced impacts on these processes; while additive white noise degrades the efficiency of synfire patterns to varying degrees, noise may conversely improve signaling fidelity for firing rate transmission at moderate levels. Additional simulations suggest that neuronal network dynamics extend beyond mere excitotoxic load, indicating the underlying process is also susceptible to staitstic fluctuations from neurotransmitter events. Subsequent comparisons of the results from deterministic (noisy connections or all random coupling) to fully random coupled networks reveal inherent distinctions between these two models. Furthermore, the role of inhibitory interneurons was also analyzed to show their pivotal contribution to forward signal transmission alongside excitative cells.

Channel estimation for Millimeter Wave and sub-Thermal frequencies within Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) environments presents a formidable challenge due to Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) phenomena. These frequencies exhibit sparsity in space-time, typically characterized by a small number of dominant paths. While Algebraic Low-Rank methods utilize space-time patterns to estimate channel eigenmodes via recurrence of vehicles traversing a specific zone, they demand extensive data—including vehicle locations and hundreds of revisits per position—resulting in high computational costs and excessive signaling overhead. This study proposes a Deep Learning approach that infers channel eigenmodes from pilot Low-Rank matrices alone, operating within dense V2X settings and requiring no location data for vehicles. Simulated results confirm that the proposed technique matches the Mean Square Error (MSE) performance of traditional position-based estimation of low rank models. Additionally, our model demonstrates the ability to transfer learning from one layout to others without explicit tuning procedures. This adaptability allows the system to apply consistent high accuracy with variable spatial-time signal variations across various urban situations, facilitating seamless deployment.

The surge in social media usage has driven a significant rise in communication via platforms such as blogs, Facebook, and Twitter, shifting initially English-dominant interactions into multi-lingual exchanges. Today, individuals often merge their natural or mother tongue languages with English, manifesting as code-mixing—whether English is romanized in other scripts or the native language's script itself remains intact. Consequently, extracting sentiments and flagging offensive content within these code-mixed microblogging tweets has become an imperative challenge in the current era. We are introducing a functioning model for Task II of the HASOC Offensive Language Identification sub-track focused on "DravidianCodeMix" presented at The 4th Evaluation Lab Conference (Forum for IR) in 2020. Designed as a classification problem at the message level, our approach employs a classifier grounded in embedding techniques to distinguish between offending benign comments on the official task data, specifically the provided Manglish dataset.

All-sky instruments can determine the brightness of astrophysical objects by detecting fluctuations in observed count rates whenever those sources are blocked by Earth's shadow; methods similar to those used by $\textit{CGRO}$-BATSE and $\textit{Fermi}$-GBM have been standard practice in this domain. This study marks the inaugural application of this occultation technique to flux measurement using a collimated setup: the Cadmium Zinc Telluride detector aboard the $\textit{AstroSat}$ mission, which relies on selecting high-fidelity occultation data to accurately derive fluxes for the Crab Nebula and pulsar, as well as Cyg X-1. The results indicate that CZTI is capable of performing such measurements for hard sources possessing intensities of approximately 1 Crab.

The integration of large electric loads and distributed generation presents challenges to the reliable functioning of low voltage distribution networks by necessitating robust operations. This research evaluates various existing techniques based on voltage and power measurements, applying them using open data across diverse levels of smart meter penetration and different accuracy standards. Analysis shows that generally higher accuracy is achieved with smart meter voltage readings compared to power readings of identical classification. If power data exists alongside it, the proposed ensemble technique further enhances the identification accuracy initially achieved with voltage measurements alone.

This thesis advances the theoretical frameworks regarding algebraic cycles and moduli spaces specifically within the domain of real numbers. In analyzing subvarieties of smooth real-projective algebraic varieties, the cycle class map—bridging the Chow ring to the equivariant cohomology ring—is of significant importance. While describing the general image of this map remains challenging, this work offers a thorough examination of the associated group for real abelian varieties. By establishing integral Fourier transforms applicable to the Chow rings of abelian varieties over any field, the study confirms the integral Hodge conjecture regarding one-cycles on complex Jacobian varieties, in addition to proving that the real integral Hodge conjecture holds modulo torsion for real abelian threefolds.

Furthermore, possessing moduli spaces for real varieties proves essential to the theory of real algebraic cycles and various other applications in real algebraic geometry. Understanding the topology of a real moduli space yields complementary insights into the geometric properties of the real variety corresponding to each point. We demonstrate that the set comprising moduli points linked to abelian varieties that contain a subvariety of a specified fixed dimension is dense within both the moduli space of real abelian varieties and the embedded Torelli locus. Also provided are the characteristics of the moduli space for stable real binary quintics, which features a hyperbolic orbifold structure concordant with the period map on the locus of smooth quintics; thereby, this space is identified with a non-arithmetic ball quotient.

Current research largely focuses on evaluating whether real-world evidence (RWE) derived from non-randomized, observational studies can yield conclusions aligned with randomized controlled trials (RCTs), a key goal of the RCT DUPLICATE initiative. To harmonize findings from an observational study with an RCT or different operational datasets, minimizing disparities in population characteristics is essential. We present an efficient algorithm grounded in network flow theory to generate well-matched pairs from observational data that align with specific target population profiles, such as RCT eligibility criteria. We apply this method by examining inconsistencies in results regarding hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for women's cardiovascular Health Initiative (WHI). While adjusting only for cardiovascular risk did not resolve the conflict between the HRT findings in trials versus the corresponding observational data, the disparity disappeared when further adjustments were made for age at HRT initiation and prior use of hormone combination products. Finally, the methodology is incorporated as part of the R package match2C.

This study focuses on Data Assimilation (DA) problems solved via Partial Differential Equation (PDE)-based methods using variational approaches or Kalman filters. Introduced briefly is the DD-DA framework, which decomposes the physical domain in both time and space to integration Schwarz-type techniques and parallel time algorithms. This paper addresses scenarios with nonuniform and generally non-uniform sparse observations using the DyDD algorithm. Few-shot classification necessitates deep neural networks to acquire generalized features from a small number of training examples, presenting a challenging yet crucial task in data-scarce settings. While recent approaches leveraging CLIP have achieved impressive results by utilizing contrastive language-image pre-training, the influence of large-scale pre-training in compensating for limited data and aiding representation learning warrants further investigation. Address this, the authors present CoMo, the Collaboration of pre-trained Models, which aggregates diverse prior knowledge from distinct pre-training strategies to enhance few-shot learning performance. CoMo integrates three key components: CLIP's language-contrastive information, DINO's vision-contrastive information, and DALL-E's language-generative capabilities. The method operates through two primary mechanisms: few-shot synthetic data expansion and knowledge ensemble. Specifically, CoMo utilizes zero-shot captioning by DALL-E to generate artificial imagery that enriches the small training set without requiring human input, alongside the use of a learnable Multi-Knowledge Adapter (MK-Adapter) to dynamically fuse the predictions originating from both CLIP and DINO. By synergizing different pre-training paradigms through this collaborative framework, CoMo maximizes their potential and achieves state-of-the-art performance on few-shot classification. Extensive experiments across 11 different datasets validate both the effectiveness and generalization capabilities of this approach.

Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) rely on functional composition, using intermediate GP layers to warp inputs, thereby enabling the modeling of non-stationary behaviors. Recent literature identifies two primary DGP regimes: a "big data" approach dominant in machine learning that utilizes optimization-based inference for rapid, high-quality forecasting, and a "small data" approach tailored to computer surrogate modeling that employs posterior integration for robust uncertainty quantification. This approach yields a substantial speedup over current exact and approximate methodologies used for gap calculation.

Data separability, a thoroughly researched issue, poses significant challenges to the estimation and analysis of binary outcome models. Definition of Done (DoD) is a core tenet of Scrum that encapsulates the Scrum Team's collective agreement on the conditions required for a product increment to be complete. These are often structured as checklists containing criteria such as software quality requirements or activities essential for the increment's deployability (e.g., coding assessments, verification steps). However, understanding their practical utility remains under-explored in academic literature. The primary objective was to investigate the specific benefits, inherent challenges, and creation-maintenance strategies associated with DoD in Agile initiatives. To this end, a global survey gathered insights from 137 practitioners working in various Agile software development environments. The outcomes reveal that while 93% of respondents found DoD valuable for completing work artifacts, guaranteeing quality, and ensuring necessary actions occur, every other surveyed project reported issues such as unrealistic, erroneous, inaccessible, or constantly evolving DoD definitions. Consequently, findings indicate that while DoD holds critical importance for Agile projects, effective utilization presents difficulties, necessitating further empirical research to establish proven best practices.

Mixture models stand out in sports analytics for their capacity to uncover latent variables. Despite their interpretability and scalability, traditional finite mixture models often rely on rigid, assumed parametric distributions for outcomes tied to these latent factors. This paper introduces a more adaptable solution allowing the latent conditional distribution to function as a mixture within Gaussian mixtures itself. Furthermore, it successfully categorizes the data into six distinct return style categories.

Visual relocalization, a central challenge in 3D vision, involves estimating a query image's 6-degree-of-freedom (6 DoF) pose within a known 3D map, a task crucial for robotic navigation and augmented reality in extensive indoor spaces. However, camera motion often triggers rapid environmental appearance shifts, posing significant difficulties for these systems. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce RenderNet, a virtual view synthesis method designed to enhance the database with synthesized perspectives for improved positioning. Rather than generating full-realism images that depend on high-fidelity 3D models, RenderNet specifically renders global and local features of virtual viewpoints, which are subsequently utilized for image retrieval and feature matching. This approach substantially boosts performance in large-scale indoor scenarios, particularly demonstrating gains of 7.1% and 12.2% on the Loc indoor dataset.

Offline reinforcement learning seeks to train policies using static, pre-collected data, eliminating the need for further environmental interactions. This setting confronts two primary hurdles: (1) extrapolation errors stemming from valuation state-action pairs scarce in the training data, and (2) distribution mismatches between the behavior policy and the inference strategy. We mitigate these issues by imposing conservatism, which ensures learned actions remain near those present in the behavior dataset. Building on recent advancements with latent action space models, we employ a distinct Normalizing Flow variant to construct a generative model that functions as an action conditioner capable of enforcing conservatism. This flow encoder is first trained under the hood supervised learning on the offline dataset, after which the latent-policy controller undergoes reinforcement learning training. This methodology prevents the generation of actions beyond the training distribution's scope entirely, rendering separate penalizers for out-of-dataset actions redundant. Evaluations across diverse locomotive and navigation tasks demonstrate that our technique surpasses other recently suggested methods utilizing generative action models across a substantial fraction of benchmark data sets.

Over-parameterized deep learning models tend to overfit the training data, rendering them vulnerable to minor fluctuations and out-of-distribution inputs, which degrades their ability to generalize. Various regularization techniques, including randomized data-dependence strategies like data augmentation, have been introduced to prevent models from rote-memorizing training patterns rather than learning meaningful representations. We introduce SIGN—a distinct adaptive, regularization-free approach—that replaces arbitrary input perturbations by evaluating individual feature contributions and applying linear mappings. By transferring data to an altered feature surface where non-pertinent dimensions carry minimal weighting, our method prioritizes robustness. We evaluated this across three distinct datasets using four different model architectures, assessing performance metrics such as classification accuracy, uncertainty estimation, out-of-distribution resilience, and corruption robustness. Results demonstrate that compacting class representations with SIGN significantly enhances the model's capacity to handle random noise and distribution shifts without compromising—and indeed surpassing—the accuracy observed on standard clean data. Furthermore, our experiments confirmed that samples generated by our technique can be effectively transferred and utilized across different model architectures.

In recent years, international collaborations have driven the creation of realistic space weather forecasting models to simulate conditions on the Sun and throughout interplanetary space. To quantify the effectiveness of these tools and facilitate model validation, cross-comparisons, and the monitoring of progress, a suite of metrics has been developed through which models' capabilities can be assessed against one another.

Bloch's theorem forms the cornerstone of topological band theory, establishing a significant epoch in quantum materials research. We provide constraints on cosmology regarding the sum of neutrino masses relative to their lifetimes, within a specific scenario where neutrinos, once non-relativistic, decay into dark radiation. In this context, data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryonic acoustic oscillations (BAO), and (uncalibrated) Pantheon supernova luminosity distances impose the restriction $\sum m_\nu< 0.42$ eV at a 95% confidence level, improving upon the 2015 Planck limits yet remaining a loose constraint compared to those for stable neutrinos. We highlight that this gain is primarily due to higher precision low-$\ell}$ polarization measurements from Planck 2018, yielding tighter bounds on $\tau_{\rm reio}$ and $A_s$. These improved measurements help decouple the degeneracy caused by the extensive influence of large neutrino masses on CMB power spectrum amplitudes.

Attention mechanisms are pivotal to natural language processing systems, particularly recurrent neural networks. Recent debates focus decisively on whether intermediate activation layers reveal the reasoning behind model outputs or improve our understanding of these systems. While a recent study by Jaiman and Walls (2023, referencing the title and arguments rather than the authors to maintain focus), argues that "Attention is not Explanation," we contest several of its premises. Our argument is that any claim hinges entirely on how one defines "explanation" and demands rigorous experimental designs that account for the entire architecture. To answer when or if attentions can truly provide explanations, four new approaches are proposed. These tests encompass a uniform-weight heuristic baseline, variance estimation via repeated random seeds, diagnostics via froze layer settings from pre-learned models, and an adversarial approach to training attention end -to -ends. These tests enable reasonable interpretations of attention in Recurrent Neural networks. Furthermore, our research finds, even in scenarios of well-found adversarial methods, reliable testings often fail to outperform the new approach's simple test on the new baseline, which does undermine validity. Such findings disprove the disproof, suggesting that attention remains a beneficial option of explanation methods.

The introduction of the open-source software package SolidStateDetectors.jl enables users to compute electric field distributions, simulate charge carrier drift, and generate corresponding detector pulses, with a particular focus on semiconductor devices. The tool supports full three-dimensional calculations as well as symmetry-based optimizations to simplify modeling. To accommodate the influence of external components, options for studying detector environments are also included. Developed in Julia, a performance-optimized and accessible programming language, the package is designed for efficient, parallel execution. Special emphasis was recently demonstrated when verifying the code against an n-type segmented point-contact germanium detector. Future development goals for SolidStateDetectors.jl are also briefly discussed and provided.

As genome sequencing advances, the incremental assembly of more precise reference genomes enhances the sensitivity of read mapping and subsequent analyses like variant detection. Achieving greater sensitivity in these downstream analyses is essential for comprehensively understanding genome donors, such as their health profiles. Ideally, reads from sequencing samples should map to the most recent reference that best suits the target population. However, the growing volume of genomic data makes the process prohibitively expensive if every read set required re-mapping to an updated reference each time improvements occur. Although various tools strive to expedite remapping between references, reads aligning to regions in an older version that lack reasonable similarity in a newer version cannot be remapped, causing state-of-the-art tools to discard significant annotations as a side effect. To overcome this major limitation in existing solutions, we introduce **AirLift**, a rapid and robust method for transferring alignments across different genome builds. In contrast to traditional full re-mapping approaches, AirLift reduces the execution time required for remappers between two reference generations by a factor of up to 27.4x, while retaining accuracy; our validation against GATK confirms its effectiveness in pinpointing true ground truth SNP and INDEL variants.

Building on previous literature's adaptation via the Newton-Cartan formalism to the Schwartzchild metric, our analysis examines two geometries: one torsional and one non-torsional. The transport trajectories evaluated consist of circular geodesic loops, non-orthogonal radial and geodesic loops, as well as a stationary and a non-relativistically timeless orbit path. After comparing these across the three geometries and summarizing their distinct features with corresponding mechanisms, a notable distinction emerges regarding a fundamental performance compromise between the torsional and non-torsional models specifically in the framework; specifically, the torsional approach offers greater accuracy for the resulting equations of motion, whereas the torsion-less model precisely captures relativistic effects.

Research has identified an entirely new class of vulnerabilities in how differential privacy is practically implemented. These issues stem from the mismatch between finite-precision arithmetic used by computers for basic operations like calculating sums—where data is represented as `ints` or `floats`—and the ideal infinite precision arithmetic (over reals or integers). This discrepancy significantly inflates the calculated sensitivity (the degree a single person's data influences a result). As a result, virtually all existing differential privacy libraries fail to add sufficient noise to guarantee privacy, leaving real-world query systems susceptible to attacks capable of extracting individual-specific information. Alongside detailing these flaws, this work offers corrective solutions by modifying or restricting sum implementations to regain the intended sensitivity bounds.

LiDAR-basedmapping within self-driving and robotic contexts presents both significance and complexity, particularly in addressing global point cloud registration issues. To resolve these challenges, DeepMapping simplifies complex map estimation through the self-supervised training of basic deep networks. Although it performs well across small datasets due to its broad convergence range, DeepMapping fails to yield satisfactory outcomes on large-scale datasets comprising thousands of frames. This limitation stems from insufficient loop closures, lack of accurate cross-frame point correspondences, and sluggish convergence within its local localization network. We introduce DeepMapping2, which incorporates two new methods to overcome these hurdles: organizing training batches according to the map topology established by loop closures, and employing a loss function based on pairwise registration to enforce local-to-global point consistency. Experiments and ablation studies on public datasets—including KITTI, NCLT, and Nebula—validate our approach's efficacy. We plan to make our code publicly available.

Vision-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) relies on visual observations but is significantly compromised by variations in lighting. Our primary strategies for successfully translating thermal imagery into dense embeddings utilize normalized 14-bit raw sensor values, hallucinating high-fidelity visual features into the pipeline, and performing feature selection to derive MDN parameters. Complementing these advances is a dedicated algorithmic camera descriptor designed within our processing loop. Experimental evaluations leveraging self-generated indoor ground and hand-held data and the public SubT tunnel dataset highlight the effectiveness. Finally, we confirm that our method enables stable accurate system operation regardless of adverse conditions.

This research explores delivering ultra-reliable, energy-saving, wireless virtual reality (VR) for mobile users. By combining millimeter waves (mmWave) and coordinated multipoint (CoMP) technologies, the study targets reliable transmission of ultra-high-definition frames and an enhanced immersive experience for these users. Due to dynamic user mobility and changing channel conditions, the study models the experience enhancement issue as a difficult sequence-dependent mixed-integer convex problem aimed at maximizing users' presence feeling (FoP) within strict limits on power consumption at both access points (APs) and head-mounted displays (HMDs). Addressing its inherent complexity, caused primarily by limited user tracking accuracy and problem structure flaws in existing methods, the study introduces a parallel Echo State Network (ESN) learning approach. This ESN method separately trains on fresh, as well as past, user tracking samples. Using the outcomes from this training, the study advances a solution based on deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for optimization. In this strategy, Deep Neural Networks (DNN) act as both the generator of integer decision parameters as well as the provider of continuous power levels to validate said integer choices against a defined criterion (reward). The scheme was then verified empirically by contrasting it to alternative algorithms through benchmark standards as well as analyzing other parameters' impact on system output. In total, the analysis of simulation results prove that this proposed scheme reduces energy drain/cost about 4.14% from all compared algorithms in this research context.

Challenging issues such as sparse data sets, inherent biases, and experimental noise frequently hinder the integration of deep learning in chemical and materials science. Transfer learning has emerged as a robust method for mitigating data shortages, while leveraging quantum calculations facilitates the creation of diverse training sets that remain resilient to the noise typical of experimental databases. This study introduces a specific transfer learning strategy for estimating solvation free energies, fusing theoretical foundations from quantum calculations with the precision offered by experimental measurements. Our architecture employs a directed message-passing neural network (DPNPnn) to encode the structures of both solute and solvent molecules. Key benefits are demonstrated through our model, particularly when dealing with limited small-scale experimental datasets and out-of-distribution scenarios. This enhanced generalization capability extends effectively across new solvents, novel elemental constituents, and heavier solutes, while improving predictions for species with higher molecular weights and weights up the molar mass. Nevertheless, the final performance of these pre-trained models remains constrained by the aleatoric uncertainty present within the noisy experimental target values. Utilizing a random test partition, we attained a mean absolute error of 0.21 kcal/mol, marking substantial progress over the baseline quantum calculations, which yielded an error of 0.40 kcal/mol. When the evaluation shifts to a curated subset of higher-quality experimental data, the achieved error diminishes further to just 0.09 kcal/mol.

Label noise is ubiquitous in various tasks such as label correction and self-training methods. Many existing methods that employ heuristics, for example based on loss levels of samples, may have limited capability under optimization. Although meta learning can improve sample-selection, optimization is expensive and time-consuming. Given the issues above, we utilize the selection-enhanced noised label training method (SEN) for label correction and self-training without employing meta learning but with a model driven-data method. First we clean data by transferring the noise distribution to a pure labeling set then train more features and use them to classify the data. Theoretically using experiments in different areas like the sentence classification and word to code systems, we show that in different settings such as label correction and self-training our method out-performs the other methods.

Identifying similarities in structured data, particularly within graphs, is an critical challenge. While graph kernel approaches exist, Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance has gained significant interest recently because its flexibility in modeling both topological and feature properties allows it to effectively handle permutation invariance. Nonetheless, as structured data spans diverse, decentralized sources across data mining and machine learning applications, access is often restricted by privacy concerns to either individual clients or data silos. To address this barrier in distributed graph mining and machine learning, this work proposes a privacy-sensitive learning method for the node embeddings of the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy. The framework employs a distributed setting alongside local differential privacy applied in post-processing, using a Multi-bit Encoder to safeguard sensitive information and mitigate privacy risks when estimating the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy of locally trained graphs using Graph Neural Networks. Our study uses $\epsilon$-LDP to ensure robust encryption and guarantees privacy while executing graph learning, which leads to constructing noisy structural metric graphs through the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy. Our experiments demonstrate that, even amidst strong noise, these structural metric graphs perform competitively in clustering and classification tasks, comparable or even surpassing standard baselines, provided privacy protection requirements are met. This paper further provides a theoretical foundation combined with empiricism to explain the efficacy underlying the Local Differential Private GW discrepancy.

Sorting is a critical, extensively researched topic with significant implications for databases, as pre-sorting relationships often accelerates complex query processing. Although Merge Sort is a leading choice in database systems, recent developments in data centers offer a new approach: moving storage and computation to separate servers necessitates data transfer over networks. These pre-particed ranges are sent individually to the server to be fully sorted before reassembly into a complete sorted stream. Because the server processes smaller subsets rather than the entire raw stream immediately—working on blocks already somewhat organized—it consumes less CPU and adheres better to virtual memory access patterns, which are typically performance-constrained. Performance evaluations across various data stream configurations revealed a substantial reduction in runtime. Utilizing this partial sorting approach yielded a performance boost of roughly 20% to 75% compared to traditional sorting performed directly by the server on the unmodified data stream.

We introduce a general class of mean-field-like spin systems characterized by random interactions, a framework that encompasses both the Erdős-Rényer graph Ising model (on inhomogeneous dense random graphs) and the random dilation and related Hopfield model. A sufficient framework is identified demonstrating that these large systems exhibit high-probability behavior akin to those formed from averaged interaction strengths, and conversely this implies that known estimates derived from the averaged interaction system are valid. Moreover, we determine asymptotic tail behaviors for ratio moments between the system based on random interactions, where the Metropolis rates are replaced by the averaged interaction strengths, and establish the asymptotic tail behavior of such hitting times. This research extends the existing literature for an Ising model. Both the potential-theoretical and mathematical inequalities are used for establishing these proofs.

While deep learning approaches for diabetic retinopathy (DR) classification often rely on carefully architected convolutional neural networks, the specific training setting plays a significant role in prediction outcomes. The training setting is defined by interconnected elements, including loss objectives, data sampling strategies, and data augmentation techniques. By systemically evaluating these major components using the ResNet-50 architecture on the EyePACS public dataset, we identify critical factors for DR grading. Our extensive experiments demonstrate four key insights: (1) the framework\'s performance is highly sensitive to input resolution, the choice of objective function, and the composition of data augmentations; (2) employing the mean square error as the loss function significantly enhances performance according to the specific quadratically-weighted Kappa metric; (3) utilizing image eye pairs substantially improves DR grading capabilities; and (4) re-balancing imbalanced data distributions via resampling actually degrades results, contrary to expectations regarding EyePACS. Consequently, integrating these optimal configuration choices into our framework—which requires no custom network design and operates solely on image-level labels for 42,670 fundus images—we achieve state-of-the-art results, yielding a quadratically-weighted Kappa score of 0.8631 on the EyePACS test set. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of our training practices across different networks and additional fundus datasets. The project code and pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/YijinHuang/pytorch-classification.

This research introduces Variable-Order (VO) fractional calculus as a tool for modeling nonlocal solids. By utilizing a redefined nonlocal fractional-frame based mechanics with VO kinematics, the study offers a distinct methodology for characterizing materials where nonlocal effects vary with location. Constraints on defining VO are derived from the principle of frame invariance regarding the strain tensor. These principles guide the application of a VO nonlocal continuum to approximate the behavior of Euler-Bernoulli beams through strong-form governing equations generated via variational methods. The resulting VO formulation is demonstrated to be self-adjoint and positive-definite; properties that ensure the governing equations are well-posed and eliminate specific boundary artifacts—advantages that classical integral-based nonlocal elasticity methods cannot always guarantee. A critical component in advancing VO applications lies in developing methods to ascertain the VO parameters for specific physical scenarios accordingly. To add to the capabilities, a novel framework is presented, using deep learning to resolve this specific identification task, known as the inverse problem—generating VO profiles from experimental observations of a nonlocal beam system's performance. It is concluded that internal Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Network architectures adaptively address non-local boundary value problems akin to those encountered here. Furthermore, the results confirm accurate retrieval of the inverse problem's unique VO characteristics, accommodating even spatial non-local behaviors divergent from the model's original dataset distribution. Finally, though specific to the dimension of an Euler-Bernoulli beam, the VO continuum theory and deep learning methods involved remain general enough for application in higher-dimensions involving any degree-ordered (heterogeneous order) non-local boundary value problems.

The theory of cyclic descents for Dyck paths, first established by Adin-Elizalde-Roichman, exhibits the property that the count of paths corresponding to a cyclically shifted descent set remains unchanged within the full cyclic arrangement; furthermore, omitting the maximum value $2n$ reduces this construction to the standard descent set. By doing so, we offer a constructive combinatorial argument demonstrating the existence of such sets while recovering the Adin-Elizalde-Roichman definition naturally when applied to the subclass of paths comprising only up and down steps.

De Finetti theorems can mitigate this complex scenario, reducing the examination scope to scenarios exhibiting independent and identically distributed (iid) structures for the devices. This study presents two novel De Finetti theorems connecting the quantum subset of conditional probability distributions directly to de Finetti distributions—specifically, convex blends of identical independent instances that also reside within the quantum subset. Additionally, the study illustrates how one of these theorems can impose constraints on an adversary in a DIQKD setting. Finally, it is noted that achieving certain desired stronger restrictions on an adversary, such as limiting the scenario specifically to collective attacks in a straightforward manner, presents significant difficulties.

The frequency of planets surrounding ultracool dwarfs remains poorly understood. To investigate this, we executed a Guest Observer campaign using NASA's *K2* mission to scan 827 ultracool dwarfs for transiting planets. Since no transits were detected, we derived constraints on planet prevalence by simulating planets with various radii and orbital periods around our target sample, injecting their corresponding light curves into the observational data, and assessing their recovery. We then calculated the likelihood of non-detection across different occurrence scenarios and used the outcomes to establish upper limits on planet frequency as a function of planet size and orbital period. Our findings indicate that short-period, mini-Neptune- to Jupiter-mass planets are uncommon around ultracool dwarfs, aligning with trends observed in early to mid-type M stars. We have specifically constrained the occurrence rate ($\eta$) for planetary companion ranges of 0.5 to 10 $R_{\earth}$ and orbital periods spanning 1 to 26.3 days.
